We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances form an abstract structure known as a system of clouds, which in turn comprise a particular type of category called a bounded functorial category. The funtorial objects in this category represent subcategories consisting of spaces with distances uniformly bounded by a certain value. The collection of metrics on a space also forms a system of clouds, which can be used to define subclouds corresponding to particular metric constraints, such as those derived from topological dimensions $\le k$. These clouds of metrics can be used to define notions of homology and homotopy for general metric spaces, as these concepts are unaffected by certain metric distortions. Specifically, the Euler characteristic of a metric space's homotopy type is determined by its Gromov--Hausdorff distance to spaces of balls. This framework generalizes the concepts of homology and homotopy to all metric spaces, providing a continuous scale from general spaces to those with specific topological dimensions.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple integration with other microstrip and frontend components via top-layer microstrip feed for ease of fabrication and design. The antenna's measured efficiency, influenced by the loss of the substrate, microstrip feed, and residual resistance within the patch, ranges between 55.1% and 68.3% across the given frequency band. The achieved stability in pattern, impedance, and efficiency throughout the specified frequency range validates the antenna's suitability for various mm-wave applications, including array-based systems.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, which is subsequently trained using reinforcement learning to improve performance. Using this approach, the study successfully applies a reinforcement learning technique to improve the fault-tolerant decoding process, surpassing previous results and demonstrating the feasibility of training devices to correct errors in complex quantum circuits, even those employing faulty Bell pair distillation for noise mitigation.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by detecting an abnormal signal embedded within noise. A new method utilizes the Baysian paradigm to estimate the signal to noise ratio of an abnormal signal within noisy data. We apply this approach to both classical and quantum states, and find that the Baysian estimate for quantum states is subject to the same constraints as a fundamental measure of interferometric precision known as the Q-factor. We further demonstrate that our Baysian estimate can outperform the standard Baysian method used for signal estimation, and find that our approach is consistent with established relationships between quantum metrology and thermodynamics. We validate our results through both numerical simulations and experimental implementation, which we demonstrate using a design compatible with closed-loop feedback systems. This work has significant implications for the improvement of quantum and classical precision measurement techniques.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Specifically, hadrons carrying an increased share of quark momentum relative to $p$$+$$p$ collisions are produced in Au$+$Au collisions. Hadrons with lower momentum fractions in Au$+$Au collisions are actually suppressed. This study demonstrates that high-momentum-fraction hadrons are not systematically suppressed in heavy-ion collisions and some of these particles may be generated during the early stages of collisions, retaining $p$$+$$p$ collision characteristics.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without traditional two-qubit gates by utilizing an inherent, always-active connection between qubits. Building on this principle, we explored the digital-analog simulation of fermionic systems, starting with an exact map of single-particle Hamiltonians and accurate simulation of two-particle interactions using a specific connectivity structure. For a given number of qubits, we established the minimum connection requirements for efficient digital-analog simulation of both fermionic and bosonic systems. Results show that a linear qubit arrangement works best for bosonic models, while a specific loop structure is ideal for fermionic models.

A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, as they either over- or under-penalize the model's predictions. 

We introduce an approach that begins with networks initialized using a comprehensive feature set, allowing even basic models to achieve improved performance and generalize better. This method takes advantage of the rich representations, leveraging them for an initial boost before refining the model as needed. 

We develop a novel initialization technique that generates a broad feature set specifically for neural networks, drawing from a controlled Laplacian distribution. This approach yields surprisingly good results, surpassing state-of-the-art OoD methods while also offering a more efficient training process that saves significant time. 

Our novel generalization tool, dubbed 'L2S', demonstrates a direct correlation with both neural network performance and its ability to handle OoD scenarios. Moreover, the initial representations exhibit a 'generalization gradient,' with an increase in diversity indicating a potential drop-off in performance. 

As an added benefit, L2S also facilitates the identification of OoD scenarios through an intuitive boundary, allowing the system to make more informed decisions on when to rely on the initial representations or switch to the learned ones to maintain reliability.

Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index, unpredictable light scattering, and speckle noise generation. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm (WMA-GA) with an R-squared-based fitness function that enhances image clarity, precision, and rapid convergence in forming complex structures within scattering media. As a companion tool, we present a data-processing algorithm capable of refining and accelerating the data-set mutation, accommodation, and optimization processes. Notably, our approach successfully transformed a conventional 63x numerical aperture (NA) system into a super-resolution 79.5x NA system, surpassing the fundamental limitations of its design.

We conduct the first thorough examination of policy knowledge transfer between a training and a testing environment. Unlike prior research, where the testing distribution is often known, our case study involves a large online marketing firm with a testing distribution that is costly to observe. Consequently, they cannot utilize empirical distribution approximation methods. Instead, we employ a model-based knowledge transfer technique that relies on a transition model trained separately. Notably, we also address a related issue known as off-policy counterfactual reasoning, where we estimate a reward function from a trained transition model and use it to evaluate the actual policy being implemented.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers during fabrication. In this study, researchers investigate the active sensor depth using the CLICTD technology, a small collection-electrode monolithic demonstrator. Particle beams are utilized to analyze the charge collection properties and device performance across different thicknesses under various beam angles. In CMOS sensors utilizing a high-resistivity Czochralski substrate, a notable enhancement is observed, with the sensitive volume increasing threefold and corresponding gains in hit detection efficiency and spatial resolution.

Advanced telescopes strive to spot planets around stars, but a limitation hinders them - their ability to see beyond the star's glare.  Aiming to overcome this, scientists are exploring new technologies and techniques.  Among these, using wavefront sensors that adjust the path of light to sharpen the image, and segmented mirrors that adjust in real-time, are key components.  Despite these efforts, finding planets around close stars and small ones remains challenging.  A new proposal suggests combining these systems with artificial intelligence to improve the image processing, and using multiple detectors to capture images quickly and accurately.  A proposed new instrument, called the "Giant Segmented Mirror Telescope," enables these improvements, and could potentially lead to the discovery of planets around thousands of stars, and even tiny ones, like red dwarfs.  A new demonstration project in Hawaii is testing its effectiveness, and a new generation of telescopes is envisioned to further expand its capabilities, potentially discovering hundreds of planets around stars and small ones, and even planets beyond our solar system's borders.

This study presents a novel exogenous model to tackle the challenge of negative interest rates, maintaining the mathematical ease of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, and incorporating the average swap rate, a average volatility measure. The legacy CIRX model, utilizing the difference between two separate CIR processes, is enhanced by integrating the ergodic ULTR short rate model. The hybrid CIRX model averages the difference between the CIRX and ULTR short rate, displaying superiority in addressing the phenomenon of negative interest rates. The hybrid model matches the average swap rate and mean short rate, offering a precise match for mean variance swap calibration, especially when exposed to the ergodic ULTR short rate, providing a straightforward adjustment for the H2C model. The hybrid CIRX model provides a precise match for H2C swaption calibration, both mean variance and plain vanilla, and outperforms the CIRX and H2C models in praxis, particularly when dealing with negative interest rates.

Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations using active neutrinos may also provide essential insights into the properties of sterile neutrinos, which could be crucial in the context of future experiments such as DUNE. We analyze how determining the active sterile mixing parameters for one type of neutrino will affect our understanding of neutrino oscillation probabilities and parameters within the three-neutrino framework. Our study covers a range of scenarios, from the hypothetical case where there is no active sterile mixing at all, to more realistic scenarios where there is some level of mixing. We draw conclusions about the potential impact on the predicted values of parameters such as the neutrino mass splitting $\delta m_{31}^2$ and the mixing angles $\theta_{3}$ and $\theta_{13}$ within the three-neutrino framework, and the parameters governing the stability of long-wavelength sterile neutrino decays, which could influence the outcomes of long-baseline neutrino experiments such as DUNE.

Meta-analyses that include multiple trials with a small number of studies may experience issues with heterogeneity, which is compounded by the potential biases introduced by weighted averages. Although using a cluster-robust variance estimator can provide improved accuracy in such cases, this benefit comes at the cost of increased computational complexity and the need for heightened caution due to the non-normality of test statistics, even when the number of studies is small. In this research, we develop two new cluster-robust estimators that outperform the existing Huber-White estimator and are computationally efficient. Our findings suggest that these new estimators are robust across various scenarios of heteroscedasticity and model specifications, outperforming the Huber-White estimator by 10-20% in terms of efficiency. Furthermore, we show that these estimators are capable of handling a large number of clusters, extending beyond the traditional limitations of diagonalization.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for a smaller time step for resolving particle collisions, traditional models often incur a high computational cost. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening the collision time, leading to inaccuracies in simulations. Our new method utilizes a multiple-step Runge-Kutta technique, combining it with a dynamic time-step adaptation approach. This method accurately accounts for collision events, resulting in improved simulation efficiency and accuracy. Our framework includes techniques such as time-step splitting, adaptive collision time adjustment, pair-wise collision modeling, and time-averaging. The method can be applied to a broad range of collision models and has been successfully validated against various benchmark tests. Its effectiveness is demonstrated in several complex scenarios, including particle sedimentation, turbulent flow, and gravity flows.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has shed new light on the particle number definition, particularly as it relates to conservation laws. Research has found that particle radiation is not a product of gravitational force-driven pair creation, but rather an outcome stemming from disparities in the laws governing particle number definition. In the far distant future, the source of emitted energy corresponds to zero-point fluctuations characterized by exponentially large wave numbers, prompting a reassessment of the black hole evaporation paradigm.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is investigated using various models in the color dipole framework. These models generate different values of a key coefficient that influence broadening calculations. Results obtained for parton-meson scattering cross-sections and parton transmission and suppression probabilities are compared across different models. Additionally, parton broadening is considered in the context of jet-like event shapes within jets produced in high-energy proton-lead collisions. Specifically, events with high transverse momentum and small opening angle between partons are examined to identify parton broadening and suppression patterns.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

The video explores the dynamics of a liquid jet that enters a channel filled with the same fluid. As the jet interacts with the surrounding stream, it becomes encircled by a sheath of entrained air. This sheath plays a significant role in the dynamic behavior of the jet and its penetration into the stream. Additionally, we examine the instability effects that develop on the liquid jet and the consequences of these effects on its behavior in the context of fluid dynamics.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory remains intact even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system state still poses a challenge, particularly when it comes to data inconsistencies resulting from data partitioning algorithms in distributed systems. In this research, we develop and test a technique, referred to as token transfer, to address such data inconsistencies and ensure fault tolerance in high-performance computing applications, as evidenced by our experiments with systems comprising up to 1024 cores and 16,000 processes.

The proliferation of data has transformed our daily lives, yet the abundance of information has reached staggering levels, making it impossible to fully process it all. To tackle this, the concept of information hierarchies emerges as a potential solution, allowing individuals to break down complex information into manageable parts and present only the essential details at the top level. In this study, we delve into the application of information hierarchies in consumer-facing systems, offering a framework that can help system designers create effective user experiences by exploiting this organizational structure. We also conduct an in-depth analysis of popular system interfaces, examining how they utilize information hierarchies and leaving room for improvement in existing designs.

We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we derived a formula to predict the likelihood of escape. This formula showcases how escape probability ($f_3$) changes with mass ratios ($q$) and demonstrates that lower mass ratios result in a higher escape probability. Furthermore, our simulations revealed that systems with lower mass ratios are more capable of achieving escape in non-hierarchical setups. To further understand these phenomena, we developed a statistical model that analyzes the distribution of angles in two-body subsystems. By comparing this model with corresponding observations, we gained insight into the temporal development of these systems. Our research suggests that most binaries in the Milky Way's disk are likely to have formed through the dissolution of three-body systems that allowed for binary escape.

Measurements of the nuclear modification factors of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in collisions of lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider in 2015. The study was based on data from both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions, involving a total of 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair. The findings show that suppression of both prompt and non-prompt mesons increases with the level of collision centrality, at an extent comparable to that found in previous 2.76 TeV collisions. The study also found that suppression of J/$\psi$ mesons does not vary by rapidity but decreases slightly at high transverse momentum levels above 25 GeV/$c$ when compared to lower momentum levels. The study found that suppression of $\psi$(2S) mesons is greater than that of J/$\psi$ mesons over the entire examined momentum range.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets capture suicidal ideation at different intervals, rendering suicidal prediction a challenging task. We demonstrate that incorporating Ecological Momentary Assessment data improves the predictive power of prediction models built using Electronic Health Records alone. Two models are developed: one that combines the two datasets, and another that competes with established state-of-the-art predictors using only Electronic Health Records. Our results show that the combined dataset yields a higher Area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve compared to the baseline in predicting suicidal ideation.

Our research reports a significant $\sim 5\sigma$ discovery of polarized X-ray emission within a range of 3-6 keV originating from Cassiopeia A with the IXPE. Our findings reveal a combined polarization level of $1.8 \pm 0.3$%, obtained after summing the polarization vectors from a large region covering nearly the entire remnant. By analyzing temperature and intensity gradients, we identify two distinct synchrotron emission components - one with a temperature of $\sim 3$ keV and another with a temperature of $\sim 2$ keV. We propose a central emission model comprising two components as well, comprising a central 'bubble' region surrounded by a'shell'. Our model indicates that the 3 keV component is primarily associated with the shell, while the 2 keV component has equal contributions from the shell and the bubble. We discover that the polarization degree from the 3 keV component is around $2.5\pm 1.5$%, while the polarization degree from the synchrotron component in the northeastern'shock' region we investigated is around $2.3\pm 2.1$%. Our findings suggest a relatively unordered magnetic field in the synchrotron component. We discuss how the polarization data can be utilized to infer electron density at different radii within the remnant, while also offering insights into the polarization degree as a function of radius in the northeastern '

Consider a set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ of distinct positive integers where $a_1 < \ldots < a_n$, with the requirement that only subset sums up to a size of at most $\lambda n$ be unique. Erdos originally proposed a conjecture suggesting that $a_n > c \cdot 2^n$, with the current record at $a_n > c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$. This article presents modified constraints where we choose a random set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ with integers between $1$ and $s$, where the random element $s$ is greater than $r$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$, and selects a function $f$ at random from subsets of $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ with sizes up to $\lambda n$. Here, we demonstrate the average value of $a_n$ to be greater than $c \cdot r^{7/6} \cdot 2^{n/2}$, with the constant $c$ dependent on the system. Furthermore, we offer computational evidence supporting the system. We also analyze a second model, where we choose a function $f$ at random from subsets of $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ with sizes up to $\lambda n$, and present results for both systems, including lower bounds on the smallest possible

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed.  It has been hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity, approximately following a $v_s^2=\frac{\beta}{2}+1$, may be derived from a more generalized form of non-linearly modified Einstein gravity.  Our research provides a precise foundation for this concept by deriving dense matter sound velocity, $v_s^2=\frac{\frac{3}{2}+\frac{\omega_0^2}{3}+\frac{\Lambda}{6}\pm\sqrt{(\frac{\omega_0^2}{3}+\frac{\Lambda}{6})^2+\frac{4\omega_0^2}{9}}}{2}$, based on a specific energy scale transformation.  Our findings are in line with the requirement that sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities: $v_s^2\rightarrow\frac{\beta}{2}+1$.  Our research offers a concrete foundation for matter properties in neutron stars as predicted by non-linearly modified Einstein gravity.  Our analysis confirms that the generalized Pollard-Thomson identity can be applied within non-linearly modified Einstein gravity

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space characteristics and covariance matrices. Both coherent and anti-coherent states emerge as special cases of these states, specifically squeezed coherent states and anti-coherent states. We assess the effectiveness of these states in achieving superior sensitivity in parameter estimation for both amplitude and phase measurements. Our analysis is relevant to both laser and atom interferometry applications.

During gas-liquid interfaces that are subject to irregular movement such as splashing and atomization, the resulting fluid structures can be intricate and embedded in their surroundings. In this work, we employ a technique called skeletonization to extract the fundamental information needed to represent their geometry. By applying a modified version of a previous approach designed for stationary interfaces, we successfully incorporate terms to account for fluid flow and interface deformation. As a result, we are able to represent the interface topology and kinematics simultaneously. In a series of experiments involving different types of interfaces, we demonstrate the efficacy of the technique and demonstrate its applications in understanding the dynamics of splashing events and multi-component droplets.

Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit active movement on surfaces with carbohydrate layers by rolling along them, as shown in recent studies. This phenomenon was previously proposed to be an example of viral surface metabolism, where the collection of spike proteins interacts with the carbohydrates, generating mechanical movement through a self-organizing process. This research aims to investigate in greater detail the physical aspects underlying this rolling motion, developing a theory that explains the motor's behavior, as well as validating the results using simulations to analyze the impact of various factors. The outcomes of this study strongly indicate that viral movement on surfaces is statistically certain to occur when the virus exhibits enzymatic activity.

We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. Surprisingly, U galaxies showed the same thick disk scaling relations as S galaxies, but U galaxies with a larger central bar and warped disk were more active in star formation. According to the dry merger rate obtained from the UDSR code, and taking into account factors that influence this rate, we propose that major dry mergers may have contributed to the formation of many massive, thin disk galaxies. Notably, U galaxies with a smaller central bar and less pronounced warp, tend to have higher black hole masses, which could be the result of a different merger history. We observed that U galaxies have an different distribution of bulge size compared to S galaxies. Additionally, despite S and U galaxies having similar disk masses, U galaxies were found to have more active star formation within their disks. We propose that U galaxies are more active in galactic evolution compared to S galaxies. It is also possible that U galaxies are in an intermediate phase between S and spiral galaxies. We speculate that U galaxies could be in a transitional phase due to a continuous activity of major dry mergers. It's also possible that U galaxies are in an equilibrium state, in which the effect of bar resonance on the disk is offset by the strength of the central

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Compounds composed of potassium ($A=$ K, Rb, Cs) combined with boron in a 2:1 ratio, form a hexagonal lattice called potassium boroboride (KBbIii), where potassium atoms occupy 2 of the 3 equivalent atomic sites. Due to the presence of only one crystal site occupied by the boron trihalide ($B_x$I$_{1-x}$, $x$ ranging from 0 to 1), this system exhibits either potassium isotope effect chiral phonons or rubidium island traffic due to atomic circulation in the crystal structure. The type of isotopic effect present determines the system's symmetry, either inversion or time reversal, breaking of which affects electronic properties by influencing the circulation of electrons. The symmetry, as indicated by our experiments and calculations, is present in all potassium boroboride's three polymorphs.

In insulators, Born effective charges relate to the movement of atomic positions within a frozen ionic configuration, described by a 2x2 matrix. Our study focuses on a two-dimensional insulator, group-IV monolayer MXE (where M is a group-IV element and XE is a group-X element from the chalcogenide family), which shows non-trivial band structures resulting from the interaction between atomic orbitals. Utilizing density functional theory, our calculations reveal that Born effective charges for MXE monolayers are anisotropic and non-diagonal, with their determinants approaching unity in all cases.

We are re-examining the application of the Nusselt number in the context of thermal fluctuations within incompressible fluid turbulence. By doing so, we aim to refine existing models for the dissipation of these fluctuations. A novel effort in this research involves exploring the application of the Nusselt number to the mixing process of two distinct fluids with different temperatures and viscosities. By doing so, we hope to develop a more precise model for the dissipation of their interface fluctuations. A key concept in this study is the Kolmogorov length, which serves as a spatial resolution metric for high-frequency fluctuations. By leveraging this understanding, we derive a more precise model for the dissipation rate of these interface fluctuations, which takes the form of $\chi_{\rm interface} \sim \varepsilon_{\rm diss} \delta t^{-1} \sim \varepsilon_{\rm diss} \eta^{-1}$, where $\delta$ is the interface thickness, $t^{-1}$ is the interface crossing time, $\varepsilon_{\rm diss}$ is the dissipation rate per unit volume of the fluids, and $\eta$ is the Kolmogorov length. This model is in agreement with earlier work by Prieuro and Falkovich, who suggested a different model for the dissipation of line fluctuations. Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric coefficient with a quantized value, but it lacks observable manifestations when time-reversal symmetry prevails due to opposing influences of internal and external states cancelling out. The distinctive response characteristic of a topological insulator manifests as a nonlinear magnetoelectric effect, which is essentially a Hall effect influenced by the magnetization. This phenomenon disappears under time-reversal symmetry, however the effect re-emerges in the presence of imbalance or disruption of this symmetry. The development of an experimental technique to measure the nonlinear Hall resistance of a thin film in the absence of confining magnetic fields has made it possible to quantify this effect. The results obtained confirm the presence of a significant nonlinear signal in Bi$_2$Se$_3$ films even at low temperatures. The discovered significant resistance variation in low external magnetic fields does not align with the typical behavior associated with a topological insulator's gapped state caused by a magnetic impurity.

In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, we observe chaotic diffusion as a typical trait, where it is found that modulating the time delay periodically leads to a significant enhancement of the diffusion coefficient by several orders of magnitude, especially when the modulation's map exhibits mode locking, characteristic of laminar chaos. For the first time, we establish a link between Arnold tongue patterns in parameter space and the diffusive behavior of delay systems. Contrary to expectation, this increase in diffusion is accompanied by a considerable decrease in the system's effective dimensionality.

We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018).

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This is made possible through a process known as design mining, which applies machine learning to categorize discussions as pertaining to design. This paper showcases a simple model for design mining, revealing that current methods suffer from inconsistent conclusions on various discussion types and projects. We then propose and demonstrate the effectiveness of a more sophisticated model that considers contextual information and contrasts design-related discussions with alternative interpretations, yielding a significant increase in accuracy and consistent results across different datasets and configurations.

A proposed model explains the existence of gravity, dark energy, and dark matter.
Dark energy and dark matter stem from a false vacuum state's random energy fluctuations, characterized by large-scale negative and short-scale positive pressures, respectively, representing incoherent and coherent aspects of a superfluid/supersolid state.
Gravity emerges from topological defects within the post-inflation virtual "condensate" component.
Consequently, it is anticipated that exotic particles that could explain dark matter will not be detected at the LHC.
Furthermore, it is suggested that the de Sitter horizon associated with holographic dark energy acts as a complete absorber for static detectors, given its infinite redshift effect.
As a result, thermal radiation emitted from this future de Sitter horizon may be the source of dark vacuum energy.

Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying pattern in nonsmooth optimization problems, and, in many cases, identifying this structure is a free byproduct, also enhancing the convergence rate once aligned with that of the problem's optimal solution. Nonetheless, pinpointing the exact structure is not possible without adaptation. By formulating an adapted constraint, our approach, ExtraProx, enables the direct optimization of the proximal component, uncovering the underlying sparsity pattern and simultaneously improving the convergence rate. Experimental results demonstrate that ExtraProx not only identifies sparsity long before other methods but also achieves improved performance, as evidenced by enhanced test-set accuracy on EXAMP, a benchmark platform for sparsity identification.

We are introducing a new concept called weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with identity, which serves as an extension to the existing notion of weakly prime ideals. A prime ideal $I$ in a ring $R$ is said to be weakly $1$-absorbing if for every three non-unit elements $a,b,$ and $c$ in $R$ where their product is non-zero and within $I$, it follows that either one of the elements is within $I$ or the product of the other two is within $I$. Our research aims to explore the relationship between this new notion and other existing concepts such as weakly prime ideals, while also discussing its properties and identifying examples. Moreover, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for an ideal to be classified as a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal in terms of its correspondence with zero sets, as well as its relationship with ring operations. Additionally, we examine the relationship between this new concept and the properties of elements within the ring, specifically prime elements, weakly prime elements, and $V$-elements. Finally, we utilize these new notions to categorize rings based on specific properties, such as rings in which all non-zero elements are prime, rings in which all non-zero elements are weakly prime, and rings in which every non-unit element is a $V$-element.

We present new findings for the branching fractions of $B^0$ and $B^+$ decays into various mesons. Specifically, our results for the branching fractions are as follows: The total branching fraction for $B^0$ decaying into $\eta$ and $\pi^-$ is estimated to be $(3.36 \pm 0.23 \pm 0.26 \pm 0.12) \times 10^{-4}$. Furthermore, the total branching fraction for $B^+$ decaying into $\eta$ and $\pi^0$ is calculated as $(6.2 \pm 1.3 \pm 0.3 \pm 0.2) \times 10^{-5}$.

Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thereby enhancing sensitivity while minimizing device complexity. Furthermore, our approach boasts a reduced footprint, polarization-insensitivity, and capability for multi-channel operation, showcasing its applications in a range of spectral domains from THz to mid-infrared.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies. This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field.

Several local governments face challenges in deploying advanced automated
evaluation of road damage due to a lack of necessary infrastructure, expertise,
and financial resources for sophisticated technology. While photo surveying offers
a more cost-effective solution compared to manual assessments, the quality of the
images collected can hinder the accuracy of the damage detection process. This
research aims to improve automated road damage detection and estimation by leveraging
deep learning algorithms to analyze low-quality images, such as those affected by
illuminance, geometric transformations, and compression. By enhancing the robustness
of these algorithms against such image distortions, we strive to increase the
precision of damage detection and estimation models. To achieve this, we conduct
a comprehensive analysis of different pre-processing techniques and data augmentation
strategies to improve the performance of deep learning algorithms for road damage
evaluation. Our findings suggest that combining a specific pre-processing method
with data augmentation can significantly enhance the robustness and accuracy of the
models in analyzing distorted images. This improved robustness allows these
models to accurately identify road damage even when they have not been exposed to
such distortions during training. By evaluating these algorithms on the CUDARoad
dataset, we discover that while they demonstrate comparable performance in terms of
accuracy for images without distortions, they exhibit notable variations in accuracy
when analyzing distorted images. This disparity in performance highlights the need
for further research into developing models that can effectively handle real-world
photo survey images collected through various cameras,

Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often rely on access to expert demonstrations within the exact same environment in which the imitation policy is to be learned.  However, when discrepancies arise between expert and agent domains due to varying dynamics, perspectives, or morphologies, imitation tasks become increasingly difficult.  This paper proposes a new framework that establishes correspondences across disparate domains using only unaligned trajectories containing states from the expert domain.  The framework leverages cycle-consistency constraints in both the state space and a domain-agnostic latent space to facilitate this correspondence.  Additionally, it ensures temporal alignment using a normalized position estimator.  The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through successful imitation learning results in multiple complex domain variations, including robots operating in micro-air vehicles and humans interacting with objects.

A major uncertainty in determining the initial mass function of the first (Population III) stars hinges on the ultimate fate of secondary protostars that form in the accretion disk - whether they will merge or remain separate. We concentrate on how the initial star formation was influenced by magnetic effects in a cosmological setting with a focus on the amplification of the magnetic field. This amplification was achieved through the initial contraction of a primordial gas cloud around $10^{6-7}$ K and the subsequent collapse of a circumstellar disk. We observe that while magnetic forces enhance the contraction of the cloud, they have a lesser impact on the disk's formation, leading to a prediction of more massive secondary protostars emerging in the early universe. Consequently, Population III stars are expected to follow a higher-mass initial mass function, more closely aligned with the standard Salpeter mass function at later epochs, when magnetic effects are taken into consideration.

Association rule analysis is a widely used technique in Data Mining. This method involves partial implications between binary variables, which can be constrained by parameters such as confidence and support levels. We delve into the concept of redundancy among association rules from a theoretical perspective. Two types of redundancy are considered: (1) structural redundancy, where an implication can be derived from another with lower support, and (2) contextual redundancy, where an implication can be obtained by combining multiple partial implications with higher support. We explore the relationship between these forms of redundancy and discuss their distinct characteristics. We demonstrate that each type gives rise to its own equivalence relation, and examine the resulting equivalence classes. Furthermore, we show that structural redundancy gives rise to a finitely representable lattice in specific situations, whereas contextual redundancy does not ensure this property. We conclude by suggesting potential approaches for managing association rule redundancy in a practical setting.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who received mental health treatment against those who did not.  A key finding reveals that receiving mental health treatment as part of probation reduces an offender's risk of returning to the justice system by as much as 17 percent over a ten-year period.  The data also indicate that receiving mental health treatment as part of probation is associated with a lower risk of violent crimes, arrest, and incarceration.  The research offers further insights into how mental health treatment within the probation system influences future criminal behavior.

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine key properties and relationships, and establish connections to other notable polynomials.

Radio maps are being explored as a promising approach to equip advanced wireless networks with situational awareness. They will likely serve a pivotal function in enabling UAV communications by allowing the assessment of signal strength and interference levels at unknown locations. Different from conventional radio map estimation techniques, which depend on uncontrolled sensor measurements, a new method proposes that a UAV collect data at designated locations along a carefully planned route to quickly obtain a reliable map. This route is optimized using a measure that identifies the most informative locations to collect data from. A novel real-time Bayesian method has been developed to constantly update the map estimate and the associated uncertainty metric with every new data point, allowing the process to take place in real-time.

This paper presents a novel approach that combines Hidden Markov Models with a Gaussian Mixture Model to identify unusual patterns in discrete time series data. The method involves using Hidden Markov Models to identify outliers, which are then grouped and further analyzed using a Gaussian Mixture Model to pinpoint specific anomalies. A clustering algorithm is employed to group these anomalies into relevant categories. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a series of numerical experiments in R, including comparisons with other established methods.

This research delves into a multi-aspect approach to person verification incorporating auditory, visual, and thermal modalities. Given the efficacy of auditory and visual modality combination, this investigation extends to exploring the effect of incorporating thermal images on verification robustness. Specifically, state-of-the-art deep learning architectures were employed to model each modality and combine them in various ways, with a particular focus on multi-modal techniques such as fusion and score-level combination. Experimental outcomes on the Modality Specific Person Verification Dataset demonstrate that a tri-modal verification system outperforms both unimodal and bi-modal approaches, with the margin being most significant for harder identification tasks. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that fusing auditory and visual signals yields the best results, with the incorporation of thermal images enhancing verification robustness and confidence.

Generating new training data through augmentation is achieved by appending existing examples to a model's training set. This approach has been successfully integrated into transformer models' training, but its effects on other models, such as Conformer, have not been explored until now. In this study, several aspects of using augmented data in machine learning were investigated, with a specific focus on the impact of continuation training with augmented data on the performance of Transformer and Conformer models. Additionally, a method for creating effective data augmentations without access to additional resources is being developed. Experimental results indicate that using continued training with augmented data improves both the robustness and performance of these models, and also reveal that different forms of continuation training have a significant impact on the performance of Transformer and Conformer models. Furthermore, a design called Binary Mask Continuation Training (BMCT) was proposed, which achieves better results compared to other forms of continuation training and matches the performance of pre-trained models while working within a resource-constrained budget. BMCT works by optimizing the model's embedding layers through a binary mask, which enables the control of data augmentation without the need for manual configuration. In experiments, BMCT outperformed comparison methods on the Speech Command Recognition, Voice Conversion, and Speech Enhancement tasks.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the parameter space $\Omega$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent and identically distributed random variables with an unknown weight or mixing distribution $m(\theta)$ that follows a known prior distribution $\pi(\theta)$ on the space $\Omega$. The estimators of the parameters $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n$ for the observations $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n$ drawn from the distribution $m(\theta)$ can be found using Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimation (GMLE). 

In this research, we establish the asymptotic distribution of the GMLE estimators $\widehat{\theta}_{i,n}$ for the mixing distribution parameters $\theta_i$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$, and prove the consistency of the kernel density estimators of the mixing distribution $m(\theta)$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$. 

Next, we propose a test statistic to investigate the hypothesis that the observations follow a specific parametric distribution $f(y|\theta_0)$ for a single series of data. The asymptotic distribution of this test statistic is established in terms of the GMLE estimators $\widehat{\theta}_{n}$ for the parameters $\theta_i$. 

In addition, we explore the asymptotic distribution of the differences between the GMLE estimators $\widehat{\theta

Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework called One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not all data records contain sensitive information. However, the previous approaches in this field made the assumption that data records without sensitive information were known in advance. To tackle this challenge, our method focuses on discovering high-confidence non-sensitive data records using reliable supervision. Guided by these principles, we propose a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) framework for handling unstructured data, and evaluate its performance on two datasets, along with an extension of existing differential privacy approaches that can work without knowing non-sensitive data records in advance. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

In protoplanetary disks, it is not uncommon to observe gas and dust emissions at different temperatures. Gas substructures, like gaps and slots, can form due to the interaction between planetary bodies and turbulent flows, which can also influence disk temperature distributions. We utilize thermal simulations of gas and dust emissions in a protoplanetary disk to investigate temperature gradients. By combining tracers of kinetic energy and entropy, we map the internal energy and enthalpy within the disk, which reveals how thermal structure is linked to turbulence-driven processes. We find that areas of gas substructures coincide with regions of altered thermal structure, which suggests that disk temperature fluctuations can contribute to its overall gas morphology. We demonstrate that a single zone model incorporating turbulence-driven processes can replicate the observed two-temperature profile in DG Canum Venaticorum, which implies that such a mechanism could apply to various astrophysical objects, including exoplanets and star-forming regions.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event acquisition rates. To overcome these obstacles, we've created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), an advanced, yet intuitive software solution that streamlines time-stamped data analysis and visualization. Leveraging an integrated approach of flowcharts and modular code snippets, our tool empowers users to perform intricate data correlation and analysis, while maintaining high computational performance and efficiency.

We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to mean field games of controls with velocities as controls. The existence of an equilibrium in this context is challenged by requiring the necessary regularity of controls to be only in L^1.

Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". Initially perceived as distinct star clusters, these structures appear to be linear formations of stars spanning hundreds of parsecs. However, a closer examination of these "strings" reveals a different story: they are actually sprawling, unbound collections of stars lacking the coherence typically seen in genuine star clusters. Moreover, the distribution of these "strings" seems to be an inherent feature of the entire galaxy, as they can be found at various distances from the galactic center. Our study focuses on one particular "string" comprising 286 wide parallel stars, which we discovered in the central regions of the galaxy. We found that these stars moved in tandem, sharing a similar anisotropic velocity vector, and were likely gathered from the galactic bulge through the process of dynamical mixing over millions of years. Interestingly, the line of sight that includes these stars lies very close to the plane of the galaxy, but the actual three-dimensional layout of the stars is more complex, as the line of sight crosses through a region primarily composed of 88% red giant stars. Given the abundance of these stellar structures throughout the galaxy, it is suggested that they are more appropriately considered as an inherent characteristic of the galaxy's overall structure, rather than as distinct star clusters.

For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker applications where users often assemble multiple garments and may accidentally pair items that don't match at all, but still look great in a specific context. Motivated by this limitation, we propose a novel Visual InCompatibility System (VICS) that scores each garment outfit with a continuous InCompatibility (IC) value. Our method leverages a two-stream Attention Network, where the first stream focuses on visual attributes and the second on visual relationships, to accurately predict IC levels. We evaluate VICS on a large, real-world dataset and demonstrate its superiority over the baseline classification method, also showcasing its practical uses for Outfit Maker applications.

The framework of quantum resource theory has significantly advanced quantum physics, enabling the unification of diverse methods to quantify specific quantum effects. These methods are distinct in their underlying principles and objectives, thus leading to a division within the theory itself. One division categorizes resources based on their generation, with free states able to be accessed for no cost, and controlled or paid for resources designated as valuable. Another separation is made based on the measurement protocol used to extract the valuable aspect of a resource. Given the intricate relationship between these categories in the theory of resource theory, a clear distinction is often challenging to achieve. This work aims to clarify the difference between the two measurements, demonstrate their distinct influence on the behavior of optimal resource achievers, and identify the consequences of each category in the context of the trade-off problem in the accumulation of quantum effects.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate of the modified FedBuff algorithm is established using stochastic gradient descent as the local optimizer.

This study introduces a functional calculus tailored to a countable set of operators generating contraction strongly continuous semigroups. We select polynomial tempered distributions as the symbol class for this calculus. We then establish a key differential property and elucidate its mapping in relation to the commutant of a polynomial shift semigroup. As a concrete demonstration of its utility, we examine the function of a countable set of second derivative operators.

Recent research suggests combining the Swampland program with dark energy's scarcity could predict the presence of an additional dimension with a characteristic scale of a micron. We've investigated how this extra dimension affects the rate of Hawking radiation in black holes and found that their perceived temperature is altered, leading to a slower radiation rate than in four-dimensional space. The impact becomes more significant at larger mass for higher-charge black holes, and an energy barrier prevents radiation below a certain threshold, similar to the particle emission process in four-dimensional space. We've also explored the stability of dark energy and black holes, finding that the latter's radiation eventually follows the four-dimensional rate, with the gap in lower-charge, larger-mass black holes.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a stable state and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surrounding water, we observe two distinct stages in its breaking process. Initially, the particles near the center of the raft move towards the periphery before slowing down and developing cracks. Further research revealed that these cracks form at a critical point on an imaginary circle surrounding the raft, and this occurrence happens earlier in weaker materials and is unaffected by the rate at which the particles return to a state of stability. This finding indicates that the breaking process of a particle raft is controlled by two separate mechanisms: one that forms cracks slowly and another that moves at a different pace, and the way in which the particles rearrange itself is not essential to understanding how cracks form.

The main challenge in developing high-performance electronic devices from gallium nitride and similar materials lies in efficiently modulating carriers. Although these materials naturally have a positive built-in electric field in one direction, known as polarization field, they lack directionality which hinders their application potential. By matching the field direction to that of the current flow in certain configurations, the performance can be optimized, resulting in faster and more energy-efficient devices. We investigated the carrier modulation in gallium nitride by stacking it on top of another nitride material with a similar crystal structure, cutting it to size, and compressing it in a specific direction. Our research showed that this kind of strain causes the bands to shift as expected, allowing the flow of holes to become more efficient while also providing an opportunity to manufacture faster transistors. We were also able to identify the optimal conditions under which the best performance is achieved, and our findings align with experimental observations, opening up new avenues for device improvement.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with a dynamic selection of support points.  By incorporating spatial correlations into the policy, our method enhances performance while adhering to environmental constraints.  Through simulations in diverse underwater scenarios, our approach demonstrated a marked improvement in learning speed and final reward achievement compared to a conventional off-the-shelf TD agent.  Even with a 90% reduction in observations, our method retained 95% of the original performance.  Future underwater field tests are planned to validate our findings.

We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that decomposes into a real function and a specific quadratic differential with a singular point. However, this differential is nonzero and holomorphic throughout the rest of the surface except at this singular point. By focusing on a patch excluding the singular point, we find new isothermic surfaces applying the Darboux and Calapso transformations. Furthermore, we investigate how the transformed patches behave as they approach the singular point and check for continuity in that region.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the Hilbert--Schmidt operator $T_p$ that maps ${\mathbb L}^2({\mathbb P}}^X)$ to ${\mathbb L}^2({\mathbb P}}^Y)$ and is defined by the conditional expectation ${\mathbb E}}^X[X|Y]$ with respect to $Y \sim {\mathbb P}}^Y$ and given $Y \sim {\mathbb P}}^Y$. It is known that $T_p$ is the orthogonal projection onto the kernel of the covariance operator $A = T_0$. We investigate the statistical approximation of the operator $T = T_p - T_0$ and show that under specific assumptions on the smoothness of the density $x \mapsto {\mathbb E}}^X[X|x]$ with respect to its projection onto the kernel of $A$, its spectral norm can be estimated up to a constant factor using the sample size $p$ and the dimensionality of the ambient space. These assumptions are confirmed for the important special case of shift-invariant densities. We implement this result to study approximations of the conditional expectation ${\mathbb E}}^X[X|Y]$. Specifically, in the regime where the smoothness of the density is limited, we show that the least-squares estimator based on $T_p$ converges at a rate of $n^{-1/p}$.

This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim-Kim on the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the first kind. We explore and define the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind and their associated properties. We derive recurrence relations, identities and present comparable results for $\lambda$-analogues of Whitney-type $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind. We also introduce $\lambda$-analogues of Dowling polynomials and provide formulas for $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind.

This research explores the idea of incorporating temporal contexts into knowledge graph embeddings to improve performance. We introduce the ConceptScope model, which incorporates facts related to the time period to enhance concepts, and vice versa. We assess the efficacy of the proposed model in a binary classification task and found that it outperforms a baseline method, achieving a Micro-F1 score of 0.947 on a dataset of scientific abstracts.

This note enhances and reinforces Bates' theorem which indicates that for row-finite graphs classified as strong shift equivalent, their associated graph C*-algebras are also Morita equivalent. This discovery opens up possibilities to investigate if the stronger notion of Morita equivalence effectively describes strong shift equivalence.

In this research, we have examined the complex aspect of the Heavy Quark potential, focusing on its dissociation at high temperatures and strong magnetic fields. Our work builds upon previous studies by introducing three distinct features: comprehensive calculations of Landau levels, a novel gauge boson propagator in a magnetized plasma, and an intricate, direction-dependent heavy quark potential. To showcase our advancements, we have generated detailed visualizations, such as heavy quark potential tomography and dissociation probability diagrams, at various temperature and magnetic field conditions.

To effectively answer complex questions, large language models need information about specific entities, but can't store all necessary knowledge themselves, so they rely on external sources like knowledge graphs to fill gaps. Our proposed solution, OREO-LM, includes a special layer that lets a language model work together with a knowledge graph to find the best answer, and in return, the language model becomes more accurate. By integrating OREO-LM with existing language models, such as RoBERTa and T5, we achieved record-breaking results and also got better explanations for the models' choices, thanks to the ability to point out relevant knowledge graph information.

We develop a method for creating high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building on the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma, we establish that a random sub-complex of a given simplicial complex will have expanded spectral properties, effectively classifying it as a high-dimensional expander. This work capitalizes on existing algorithms for embedding simplicial complexes, while incorporating techniques from probability and combinatorics to understand the properties of the constructed expander graphs. Notably, our process is algorithmically driven and quantitatively driven, enabling us to present explicit examples of high-dimensional expanders.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for specific tasks and tested them on tasks for which they were not initially intended. Our quantitative analysis across multiple fixed choice datasets demonstrates that prompts containing answer options and those not utilized during pre-training exhibit notable performance enhancements.

We have computed Benois $\mathscr{L}$-invariants for weight one cuspforms and their corresponding adjoint representations. Additionally, our calculations extend Kronecker's theorem regarding the pairs of non-isomorphic one-dimensional representations of weight one cuspforms with their conjugate fields.

Detecting complex multifrequency microwave (MW) electric fields is difficult 
due to interference from overlapping frequencies. Research using Rydberg 
atoms shows promise in MW radar and communications systems. Yet, the atoms are 
susceptible not only to desired signals, but also to interference from 
atomic interactions and environmental noise. To resolve this challenge, we've 
successfully integrated Rydberg atoms with deep learning algorithms, allowing the 
model to distinguish between intended signals and noise variables. By doing 
so, we've enhanced the sensitivity of Rydberg sensors by eliminating interference 
sources, allowing us to accurately predict changes in frequency shifts and 
amplitudes free from interference effects. We've tested this integration in 
a practical scenario of sensing multiple-frequency MW electric fields and 
found that the model accurately maps the atoms' response into meaningful data 
correlations, effectively filtering out noise variables and enhancing the 
sensor's overall performance.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is hunched forward at its center and has a significant star formation occurrence away from its axis. Although its low surface brightness makes it difficult to obtain in-depth data, a recent study using the MIRI at James Webb Space Telescope has provided a deep and high-quality thermal infrared image of the galaxy. This image, combined with data from other telescopes, has enabled researchers to analyze the galaxy's properties in detail. Contrasting its expected smooth mass distribution, the images show that UGC 8839 has a distorted and swirled mass distribution and a ring of young stars surrounded by a gas disk. This indicates that the galaxy has undergone a gravitational interaction in the recent past, likely causing the axisward side to form new stars. Despite being young, the stars in this axisward ring align in the direction of the galaxy's mass distribution, suggesting they are not part of a larger halo structure. This finding rules out the theory that young stars in low surface brightness galaxies necessarily reside in structures extending into the galaxy's halo.

For a quasiregular self-map in 3D space, research has demonstrated that the Hausdorff dimension of its fast escaping set can be any value within the range of 1 to 3. An estimated lower bound has also been proposed for the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set under a specific growth constraint.

Using the Neutral Gas Ion Mass Spectrometer on board the Mars Atmospheric and Volatile Evolution/NASA Mars Science Laboratory mission, the oscillating CO$_{2}$ density in the upper Martian atmosphere between 120 and 190~km was monitored for the first study and was correlated with magnetic field fluctuations observed by the Magnetometer on board the mission. These density oscillations, resulting from gravity waves, showed varying intensity and horizontal direction, influencing the CO$_{2}$ density to the extent of up to a 30\% variation. By analyzing their horizontal distribution, it became evident that the strongest signals reside near the equator and are primarily moving eastward. These findings revealed a link between the oscillations and the magnetic field, suggesting that the former are caused, in part, by the latter. This implies that the atmospheric interactions on Mars can no longer be dismissed as insignificant, influenced as they are by the planet's weak magnetic field.

The LHC is capable of facilitating two distinct types of interactions: proton-proton collisions and heavy ion collisions, including the latter's various sub-classes such as peripheral and ultra-peripheral collisions. Ultra-peripheral collisions occur when highly charged ions collide while remaining in their ground state, resulting in photon-photon interactions that give rise to unusual particle production phenomena, including the creation of exotic states, in addition to conventional particles like hadrons, heavy quarks and lepton pairs. Notably, data collected during Run 1 were insufficient to draw conclusions on exotic state production, but Run 2 data, along with Run 3 data expected from an upgraded LHC, are anticipated to provide crucial insights in this regard. This discussion will cover the spectrum of new physics possibilities in photon-photon interactions, focusing specifically on the production of exotic states, in addition to highlighting the distinct roles that different LHC experiments will play in uncovering this phenomenon.

Recent breakthroughs in audio generation using neural models often build upon existing work in the field, often improving upon it while introducing new capabilities. This study aims to explore sounds that resemble the hum of an engine, a distinct noise often encountered in everyday life. To create such authentic sounds, we leverage a text-to-sound approach that relies on conditioned probabilistic models. Specifically, we develop a model that combines a probabilistic model, trained on extensive data, with a condition that mimics the characteristics of an engine's hum. Our model is based on a probabilistic autoregressive model that integrates a neural network, designed to generate sound sequences. By integrating this condition into the probabilistic model, we can generate more natural-sounding sequences. Our findings indicate that our model is capable of producing a wide range of sounds, including those with pitch variations, which resemble engine hums.

Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing sequential data, including natural languages, sounds, and time-series information. In contrast to conventional feed-forward networks, they incorporate a self-referential component, enabling the retention of temporal context and the representation of long-term dependencies. This architecture has been successfully employed in a broad range of tasks, including natural language modeling, stock market forecasting, image description, speech recognition, machine translation, and object tracking. Nevertheless, several limitations have prompted researchers to explore alternative designs. Specifically, conventional recurrent units often exhibit inconsistent behavior, rendering them challenging to interpret and train. This study proposes an innovative design for a recurrent unit, dubbed the hypercomplex recurrent unit (HRU), which leverages hypercomplex numbers to facilitate internal state computations. By employing a complex-valued hypercomplex vector, the network can efficiently capture multiple aspects of sequential data, such as temporal patterns, trends, and anomalies, making it a suitable choice for tasks like time-series analysis and signal processing. Experimental validation of the HRU architecture has demonstrated its effectiveness in outperforming traditional recurrent units on benchmark datasets.

Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as modeling under specific economic assumptions often yields non-transferable results. This research investigates how implementing timely moderate measures can resolve the trade-off between medical efficacy and economic impact, and attributes this finding to the broader concept of 'economic irreversibility,' illustrating its analogy to the principles of thermodynamics. A fundamental inequality provides a framework for the implementation of such measures. A novel theoretical approach underlying this methodology contributes to the body of econophysics research.

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: identifying the influence of individual data points on the training process. This problem is linked to the long-standing issue of pinpointing sensitive data in databases. This paper addresses the issue of quantifying the contribution of each data point to the training of a machine learning model by applying the principles of cooperative games in order to determine a relative contribution to the model's accuracy. Unlike traditional applications of cooperative games, which deal with absolute values, this paper focuses on percentages by normalizing the environment to represent a standard "what if" scenario for what the model could have achieved with perfect data. We utilized three different models (linear regression, decision trees, and random forests) on two datasets to test our method, which showed promising results and offered valuable insights into the data selection process for machine learning model training.

This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices.

This study provides an in-depth examination of the pressure-dependent AHE in the antiferromagnetic compound YMo$_2$O$_5$ using transport measurements. Data show that pressure significantly enhances the AHE magnitude while suppressing the paramagnetic AHE contribution. Pressure's effect on the AHE magnitude follows a non-intuitive, nonlinear pattern and exhibits a threshold above 2 GPa. Additionally, high-pressure transport measurements reveal that the Hall resistivity is dominated by a paramagnetic term in low-pressure conditions and shifts to an antiferromagnetic contribution at higher pressures. To interpret these results, a model incorporating pressure's effect on the magnetic exchange interaction and crystal structure is necessary. This phenomenon is likely caused by pressure's effects on the MO$_6$ octahedron, shortening the $a$ axis and affecting the magnetic exchange interaction between ions. This model is consistent with the pressure-dependent AHE data and provides valuable insight into the structural behavior of magnetic compounds under extreme conditions.

Formal entities' attributes and relationships are distilled from unstructured text via Relation Extraction (RE), a critical NLP task. RE involves identifying entities in a sentence and matching their relationships with other entities.
