We introduce a novel approach that leverages a graph neural network to model long-distance dependencies and contextual interactions among tokens for RE. Our proposed method accelerates training and improves generalization by transforming tokens into entity features and relationship features through a graph encoder. These features are then combined and fed into a relationship classifier. We test our strategy on the SemEval 2014 task dataset and outperform the baseline results. Notably, this method can be applied to models beyond BERT and BERT-based variants, offering versatility and efficacy.

This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the boundary of $\Omega_0$ and the ball are subjected to non-local Steklov-Robin boundary conditions. Our analysis focuses on the behavior of the eigenvalue as the radius of the ball approaches zero.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to curate relevant substructures from the graph dataset; second, a hypergraph reconstruction algorithm utilizes these sampled substructures to construct a real-world hypergraph that captures its essential characteristics. Our approach not only addresses the lack of suitable hypergraph learning tools but also also links graph dataset analysis to the broader field of hypergraph learning, offering a new direction for related research.

In medical radiology reports, doctors document vital information about patients'
health conditions. Their findings are derived from analyzing raw imaging data and
describe the inner body structures. Preparing these reports necessitates medical
experts to have extensive knowledge of anatomy and to be familiar with their own
hospital's equipment, leading to a high barrier for entry for new radiologists.
Automating the process becomes even more challenging due to the complexity of
translating anatomical information into text. Current methods fail to effectively
incorporate anatomical details, which is crucial in medical accuracy. To address
this issue, we suggest employing anatomical information as prior knowledge in the
segmentation process of medical images. By doing so, we hope to improve the
accuracy of medical image segmentation and ultimately contribute to the development
of more precise automatic radiology report systems. In this paper, we propose a
new method that utilizes anatomical information for the automatic detection of
prostate zones in radiology images. By incorporating anatomical information as
prior knowledge in the form of structural constraints, we can improve the prostate
zone segmentation process. By using a UNet-like architecture within a Variational
Network, we leverage anatomical information to fine-tune the segmentation
outcome, thereby achieving better results compared to standard UNet-like models.
Our experiment revealed that the proposed method surpasses baseline UNet-like in
terms of anatomical information accuracy in the prostate zone detection.

Bill Thurston initially found that Euler classes of taut foliations in hyperbolic 3-manifolds have a limited range and then made an educated guess that this range is the absolute minimum. Subsequent work by a different researcher, collaborating with David Gabai, found counterexamples that contradict this theory. Due to the connection between tight contact structures and taut foliations, researchers now consider the possibility that this theory could hold for tight contact structures, which are also related to Euler classes of one. To test this idea, recent findings show that previously found counterexamples are also related to tight contact structures, leaving room for the possibility that this theory might be correct for tight contact structures.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the issue of overemphasizing high-intensity peaks. Conversely, entropy-based measurements offer comprehensive insights for more complex and real-world scenarios, encompassing broad emission patterns and diverse statistical distributions. Furthermore, we develop a theoretical model to predict entropy in microcavity lasers, illustrating its potential as a fundamental tool for designing future directional light sources.

Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter-term price fluctuations, we found that the prices of major cryptocurrencies converged with inflation rates in 2020. Our research employed two prominent methods to filter out fluctuations: the Hodrick-Prescott filter, which is widely recognized in the field, and a new approach based on quadratic splines that we developed. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of the quadratic spline method in filtering prices and identifying underlying trends.

By integrating analytical methods including field theory, probability and integrability, we resolve the large deviation issue of the KPZ equation at early time periods. Expanding the existing weak noise theory, which reformulates large deviations into a nonlinear hydrodynamics problem, we reveal its complete solvability through a link with the integrability of the Zakharov-Shabat system. Employing the inverse scattering technique and a newly developed method for solving finite-dimensional approximations of nonlinear equations, we arrive at exact solutions that depend on the specific probability distribution considered. Two prominent cases - the Gaussian distribution, resulting in the KPZ equation's exact solutions, and the Bernoulli distribution, leading to the exact solutions of the stochastic Burgers equation - illustrate the applicability of this approach.

The solar wind's compressive plasma turbulence at sub-ion scales is analyzed with data from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission. Utilizing both the Fast Plasma Investigation instrument and calibrated spacecraft potential measurements from the Spin Plane Double Probe, researchers are able to investigate turbulent patterns down to specific frequencies. These measurements are then applied to various solar wind plasma intervals. One such interval is scrutinized, yielding valuable insights into its power spectral density fluctuations spanning from the inertial to sub-ion range. Two possible explanations for these density patterns exist, suggesting that they are a result either of specific wave types and interactions at varying scales or a broader physical phenomenon, the Hall effect. These theories are substantiated through the examination of associated electric field data.

In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions. Simulation data for the FLASH facility show successful production of pulses lasting several hundred attoseconds within a 2-10 nm wavelength, yielding high peak powers of hundreds of megawatts, with a potential for delivering over a thousand pulses per second to enable groundbreaking attosecond science applications.

A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but neglect those affecting diffusivity. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are explored for this modified equation using the WKB method near critical levels and singularities, including turning points.

Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the
level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of
this approach, particularly in a real-world application involving Texas, where a
faster alternative to traditional methods yielded fairer voting distributions and
allowed for the identification of biased districting plans.

A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which integrates Gabor and HOG to precisely locate defects. Since defects distort the fabric's uniform pattern orientation, this method leverages the direction awareness to effectively identify the defect region. Following the development of a directional descriptor, the proposed technique applies low-rank decomposition to differentiate the background from the defect area, where the background is represented by low-rank matrix and the defect region by sparse matrix. A matrix-nuclear-norm regularized sparse approximation model is then employed to filter out noise and enhance the defect boundary. Ultimately, thresholding and morphological processing are used to segment the defect region from the background. Experimental results demonstrate that this method outperforms existing techniques for defect detection, presenting better sensitivity and accuracy.

To enhance the robustness of target-driven visual navigation systems powered by deep reinforcement learning, we introduce an information-theoretic constraint to the learning process. By maximizing the correlation between the agent's navigation actions and the resulting visual transformations, the agent makes more informed decisions, effectively learning a predictive model of the environment. Through a variational generative approach, we formalize this concept and implement a generative adversarial network (GAN) to simulate the agent's experience. Our method demonstrates a significant improvement in navigation outcomes for both synthetic and real-world datasets, outperforming existing DL-based approaches in uncertain and dynamic environments.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast, the conditions under which scalar gravitational waves in Brans-Dicke theory allow light to escape infinity without being overpowered by rapid mass loss.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies the nuclear star clusters' formation through the motion of these binary remnants at redshifts between 10 and 6. Following this process, our model tracks the development of these clusters until the present day. In nuclear star clusters, we find that approximately 4% of Population III binary remnants undergo a merger at redshifts above zero. These mergers produce black holes of various masses, from 40 to 1000 M$_{\sun}$, and one particular merger produces a 55 M$_{\sun}$ black hole. This type of black hole is of specific interest because it is one of the objects similar to the observed PBH candidate with a value of $\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{BH}}/\mathrm{M}_{\sun})=-0.40$. Our study also reveals that the majority of these mergers occur in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters. Additionally, we discover that the clusters' gravitational potential is insufficient to prevent the escape of a significant number of black holes formed through the merger of Population III binary remnants. We find that approximately 50-80% of these black holes escape the clusters. We attribute this to the finite number of particles used in our semi-analytical model that forms the basis of

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel data-driven method for identifying critical incidents related to ESS performance in distribution networks. Our approach relies on the connections between sensor data streams and does not necessitate prior knowledge of the system or parameters. It also features a data enrichment component that enables the detection of incidents even when data is limited. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through detailed case studies that focus on active and reactive power control strategies for ESS.

Our study focuses on how the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons contribute to the radiative decays $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$. The first process is predominantly driven by the $\omega$ meson. On the other hand, the cascade decays involving the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons are substantially suppressed compared to other competing diagrams, specifically those involving the $\psi(2S)$ and intermediate $\pi$ mesons. The observed isolation of the $\omega$ signal in experiments may be attributed to the presence of these competitive contributions.

We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months.

The study on varying Hall conductivity in Topological Insulators using a tight-binding model has revealed that edge dislocations create a unique surface state. This surface state forms a semi-circular energy contour, which increases along with the magnetic field's flux, directly proportional to the charge density of the dislocation. Notably, this surface state energy band spans the entire Dirac band gap, going from the bulk's conduction band to the surface's conducting state. This dislocation-induced surface state within the band gap robustly resists disruptions caused by random potentials, elliptical potentials, disorder, and magnetic field variations.

Consider the scenario where $p$ lies between 1 and infinity, $
u$ ranges between 0.5 and infinity, and $\mathcal{S}_
u$ denotes the set of non-zero vectors in 2D space with a polar angle smaller than $ rac{\pi}{2
u}$. We introduce $R > 0$, and $\omega_p(x)$ as the p-harmonic measure of $\partial B(0,R) \cap \mathcal{S}_
u$ at point $x$, relative to the ball $B(0,R) \cap \mathcal{S}_
u$. We show that for some constant $C$, $\omega_p(x)$ satisfies a specific non-degeneracy condition, particularly when the distance from $x$ to $\partial B(0,R) \cap \mathcal{S}_
u$ is large enough. We achieve this by utilizing a half-plane model to analyze a certain integral and making key adjustments to a classic oscillatory estimate by Carleman. We also explore the oscillation of $\omega_p(x)$ and its relationship with the distance from $x$ to $\partial B(0,R) \cap \mathcal{S}_
u$.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is examined in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2018. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing wind and wave measurements and applying an extreme value model to estimate the probability of severe storms in specific locations. Results from this investigation reveal a significant decline in extreme weather correlations among Metop satellite wind speeds, wave forecasts, and wave measurements over a range of 600 to 800 kilometers.

Inspired by intermediate Lang conjectures concerning hyperbolicity and rational points, we establish new theorems on the finiteness of non-constant morphism sets from a specific fixed variety to another, also defined over a specific number field, by adapting Faltings's work on the finiteness of maps in moduli spaces.

A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human pose data and task dependencies, enabling the identification of pose configurations that are humanly feasible and relevant. In robot teaching, learning the desired action is simplified by identifying the target object rather than specifying the exact pose. In emulation of human motion, focusing on the end-effector rather than the entire arm reduces the difficulty of replicating movements. In all these scenarios, manipulability ellipsoids serve as an ideal metric for evaluating the similarity between two points in space. This paper presents an efficient approach to computing manipulability ellipsoids for general REDIVI systems consisting of revolute and prismatic joints, as well as a set of dependent variables. The approach is based on a novel decomposition of the covariance matrix and the application of singular value decomposition. The method has been successfully tested on a humanoid robot, allowing it to navigate through the manipulability ellipsoid efficiently and accurately.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in future high-energy colliders, it is crucial to understand the total cross-section and main background processes accurately. Future colliders such as the HL-LHC, FCC-ee, FCC-hh, and CEPC will play a significant role in this research. To calculate the total and differential cross-sections for Higgs boson pair production in future colliders, it is necessary to implement the relevant matrix elements into the parton level Monte-Carlo code, NNPDF3D. We have successfully integrated the next-to-leading order strong and electroweak corrections for non-resonant Higgs boson production at next-to-next-to-leading order in the Standard Model into NNPDF3D. We present the next-to-leading order predictions for the total and differential cross-sections of Higgs boson pair production at the LHC, a 100 TeV proton-proton collider, and an electron-positron collider. We have also found that our Monte-Carlo code matches well with state-of-the-art fixed order parton level results for non-resonant Higgs boson production. We have used next-to-leading order QCD PDF fit for our calculations which matches well with other next-to-leading order QCD PDF fits. We have also found that our Monte-Carlo code matches well with next-to-leading order strong and electroweak corrections for non-resonant Higgs boson production at next-to-next-to-leading

A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D object pose estimation models, utilizing unstructured, 'in-the-wild' video footage where objects are rotated. These scenes are commonly encountered and can be easily gathered (e.g. cars navigating roundabouts, planes near airfields). The combination of traditional structure-from-motion techniques and cutting-edge object detection and feature matching methods yields surprisingly accurate 3D pose estimations in such video footage. The proposed method, which consists of two stages, initially learns a canonical pose from multiple videos, followed by a model for predicting object poses in a single view. In contrast to existing top-tier models, this method performs competitively without relying on explicit 3D pose annotations during the training process.

Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts due to misconceptions disseminated through social media regarding COVID-19 vaccines. Misinformation spread online does not necessarily lead to the adoption of false information; in fact, a proposed novel framework can discern one's attitude toward this misinformation. This new framework leverages neural networks and attitude consistency to classify stances toward COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation. A novel dataset, named AttMis, comprising Twitter conversations, provides the framework with necessary tools to navigate the complexities of stance detection in nuanced contexts. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms other neural stance detection models, including a model pre-trained on a standard COVID-19 vaccine conversation dataset.

Advancements in attosecond science hold great potential to unveil the core electronic behavior of matter, contingent on achieving higher photon energies and flux. By integrating technological innovations from free-electron lasers and table-top high-harmonic generation, we can attain this goal. Two pivotal objectives are to create attosecond X-ray sources and coherent table-top soft X-ray sources. This paper outlines the latest developments and promising strategies for making inroads in attosecond science, focusing on schemes featuring multiple optical cycles, plasma-based sources, and the fusion of photo- and electron-driven processes.

Eclipse predictions for binary stars can be significantly improved by revising ancient concepts.  Historically, astronomers believed that changes in eclipse times were solely caused by the precession of equatorial planes of rotating stars aligning with specific sky coordinates.  While this theory holds some merit, other factors like mass loss and magnetic star activity can result in periodic time changes.  In the case of Algol, one such example reveals a 72-year pattern, whereas another star, R Scorpionis, exhibits a 13.25-year cycle, both indicating non-synced magnetic activity with their respective orbital periods.  Interestingly, the binary system Algol displays an unusual 20-year pattern of fluctuations in its eclipse-observing epochs, in addition to the already known 72-year pattern.  Using advanced mathematical tools, it is proposed that these two cycles are interlinked with the binary system's long-term changes, in contrast to the commonly accepted idea that these changes are caused by precession aligning with specific star and binary system orientations.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that solutions remain bounded in a specific functional space, we derive a notable result concerning the long-term behavior of solutions, which may have significant implications for studying specific properties, particularly the nontrivialness of solutions in a functional space associated with the Sobolev embedding theorem.

Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving significant success across a range of applications, further improvements to acceleration and scalability are still needed. particular issue arises with the widespread use of Monte Carlo sampling within current algorithms based on physics-informed neural networks. Our work presents enhanced variants of existing algorithms designed to reduce the effects of noise and improve scalability by omitting the need for Monte Carlo sampling. Our methods are tested across a range of benchmark problems and deliver substantial gains in processing speed and memory efficiency.

This study examines the behavior and simulation of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs by analyzing the movement of domain walls within the ferroelectric material. The presence of domain walls leads to the negative capacitance effect, which improves the transconductance of the device. However, this domain structure also causes a domain-dependent threshold voltage issue. To investigate this issue, the study uses a combination of electronic structure simulations and microscopic models to analyze the electronic properties of the material at the domain walls, and incorporates an innovative approach to modeling domain structures. The results show that domain walls have a significant impact on the device's electrical properties, and that these properties vary depending on the orientation of the domain, leading to increased variability in threshold voltages.

A significant knowledge gap exists in understanding the Cargo ecosystem's architecture and how vulnerabilities spread throughout it. Existing studies focus on operating systems or firmware, ignoring the complex ecosystem of software components. To bridge this gap, we developed a tool to create and visualize a dependency graph of the Cargo ecosystem, allowing us to analyze software vulnerabilities. Our analysis reveals that the Cargo ecosystem is composed of approximately 800,000 projects, with vulnerabilities originating from a few key libraries, primarily due to format string vulnerabilities, buffer overflow errors, and resource management issues. We observed that vulnerabilities are recurrent, with many appearing multiple times in different libraries, and in some cases, these vulnerabilities remain unresolved for years. Furthermore, we found that vulnerabilities are often linked to outdated dependencies, and libraries contributing to system security, such as cryptography, are more prone to vulnerabilities. We also identified a significant number of vulnerabilities associated with Cargo's nightly versions, which highlights the importance of regularly updating dependencies in order to prevent vulnerabilities.

For analyzing ergodic properties in stochastic dynamical systems, it's essential to demonstrate irreducibility. This paper confirms the irreducibility of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations subjected to discrete jump noises and shows these results apply universally, imposing minimal restrictions on noise conditions. A critical factor in this study is the authors' and T. Zhang's previously established criteria for irreducibility in stochastic equations with jump noises. This proof is then utilized to demonstrate ergodic behavior in stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations and includes scenarios of weak dissipation with jump degenerate noise.

For a finite noncyclic nilpotent group G, we're analyzing the minimal vertex degree in its power graph. This power graph connects vertices based on one being a positive power of the other. By examining the group's prime divisors and Sylow subgroups, we can pinpoint the elements generating the largest cyclic subgroups within these divisions. These elements also serve as the group's minimal generators when G is a noncyclic nilpotent group with a prime-order p. We're using the group's structure to determine the number of vertices of minimal degree in its power graph.

Hadron-hadron collisions in the intermediate Feynman-x region (between 0.1 and 0.9) have not been extensively studied at high-energy ranges above sqrt(s) = 63 GeV using the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings. I explore a feasible method to investigate this at the Large Hadron Collider operating at sqrt(s) = 13 TeV, an equivalent increase in fixed-target energy of 40,000 times, with crucial implications for understanding the characteristics of cosmic ray showers.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations resistant to various transformations. However, these models are limited by their inability to differentiate between basic geometric transformations, such as orientation and perspective. This issue can be addressed by developing more advanced image representation techniques. In this research, we introduce a new concept called Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), which incorporate geometric invariance through the incorporation of Oriented Pyramid Pooling (OPP) modules. The OCNs leverage a novel encoding system that concatenates representations from multiple scales, facilitating improved feature extraction and geometric invariance. The introduction of anupp module enables the model to achieve a high level of perspective invariance. The proposed OPP modules possess three key properties: pooling, fusion, and expansion. The pooling property allows the model to capture distant spatial relationships, while the fusion property enables the model to combine representations from different scales, and the expansion property allows the model to achieve a high level of perspective invariance. The proposed OCNs outperformed state-of-the-art models in multiple tasks, including LFW incognito, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and MNIST datasets. Additionally, the proposed models demonstrated improved accuracy on low-light images and geometrically distorted images. The proposed models also exhibited a significant decrease in accuracy when subjected to synthetic orientation and perspective transformations, confirming their geometric invariance.

This study presents an optimized version of graph convolutional networks, which enables efficient learning directly from point clouds. The enhanced model achieves this by accurately reproducing the original point cloud topology through a refined graph construction method, thereby improving computational efficiency. The proposed framework replaces the traditional K-NN graph with a delta-map graph, offering a more accurate representation of point cloud geometry. As a result, the spatial relationships between nearby points are preserved, and the model's ability to distinguish between subtle and significant details is significantly improved. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated by sustained performance gains in various 3D segmentation tasks, and the code is available for reproduction at https://github.com/fatemehkarimii/graph convolutional networks.

We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses fixed images in conceptual meaning but can take various forms visually. Unlike existing Trojan attacks, which embed inconsequential triggers in clean images, our method considers trigger images as full-resolution representations of meaningful object classes. As our attack is the first to utilize irrelevant background in trigger images, it can be applied to any dataset with class labels, making the attack more versatile. We also found that using multiple classes for trigger synthesis enhances recognition accuracy and resistance against countermeasures. Furthermore, our attack can be applied to video datasets by synthesizing trigger images for each class. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three large-scale datasets, showing that even with limited background instances, the recognition accuracy of the Trojaned model can still reach up to 80.96% on CIFAR-10 and 54.15% on ImageNet.

We are developing an image slicer for an integral field unit, ROSIE IFU, to integrate with the IMACS spectrograph on the Magellan Baade Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory. The system is designed to accommodate a 3.5 arcmin diameter field of view and offer up to 13,000 spectral resolution by utilizing 9 parallel slit sections, each with a 50 arcsec width. The final product features a 9x9 array of pseudo-pixels, formed by reformatting light from the slices via a volume phase holographic diffuser and further refined by a collimator and flat-field corrector lenses. The unitization of eight IF Units, comprising six already installed and two in processing, has brought our installation plans to an advanced stage, with significant progress made towards a Baade Telescope in conjunction with Magellan project aimed at obtaining large-scale structure information via galaxy clustering analysis on a 20-200 Mpc scale.

In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments. Specifically, key experimental and theoretical findings from a 2020 review are applied to examine the various reaction processes involved in stimulating astrophysical $S$-factor values for significant energy thresholds. These developments have led to a refinement of the paper's presentation, with new energy curves for relevant resonance channels obtained via direct calculation or newly determined resonance parameters.

A crucial aspect of discovering and studying exoplanets is identifying terrestrial planets resembling Earth. New studies emphasize the significance of considering volatile depletion in star composition to predict the bulk composition and internal structures of these planets. In this research, we apply this concept to a sample of 13 stars that host terrestrial planets similar to our Sun, utilising high-precision data on their elemental composition. Based on this and other constraints, we simulated the detailed mineral makeup and internal structures of hypothetical habitable-zone exoplanets around these stars. Our model indicates that most of these planets are expected to have compositions and internal structures analogous to those of Venus and Earth. However, our analysis reveals two potential outliers: HR 259, which may host a planet much like Mars, and Kepler-10, which may host a planet with a crust composed primarily of refractory minerals and a dense interior. These findings highlight the significance of precise knowledge of a star's composition in predicting the properties and characteristics of terrestrial exoplanets.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), utilizing raw CSI to learn location-specific features. Nevertheless, several studies demonstrate that CSI is prone to system disturbances and subtle environmental changes. Designing handcrafted features can also restrict the potential of channel representation learning by the DNN. This research suggests attention-based CSI for learning robust features. The proposed approach's efficacy in centralized and distributed massive MIMO systems is assessed using ray-tracing channels in two railway environments under varying conditions, resulting in a superior performance compared to a conventional DNN.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to the topological categories theory. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors.

We investigate functions defined on the vertices of the Hamming graphs H(n,q), focusing specifically on those with support contained in the direct sum of the eigenspaces U_i(n,q), U_{i+1}(n,q),..., U_j(n,q) where 0 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n. Under certain conditions, specifically when n is greater than or equal to the sum of i and j, and when the size of the alphabet is 3 or greater, we identify the functions with minimum possible support and determine their values, discovering they are equivalent to the functions defined on the eigenspaces U_i(n,q), U_{i+1}(n,q),..., U_j(n,q) of the Johnson graphs J(n,q) with the same properties.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser. Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI mirrors COPASI's interface for seamless exploration and enables essential operations within the web environment. Users can access ShinyCOPASI at http://shiny.copasi.org/ and download the application from the bioFETIX repository at https://biofetix.org/shinyCOPASI/.

Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. Research examines not only the inherent uncertainties tied to measurement and model limitations but also the inherent uncertainties rooted in those limitations. This work presents an innovative approach applying Gaussian Process regression to quantify the uncertainties associated with NN predictions, with an added benefit of enabling the incorporation of correlations between datasets. This framework has been successfully put to the test on data originating from experiments and simulations, in particular, for computing properties of polyatomic molecules and simulating turbulent flow characteristics.

We prove that quantum group unitaries for compact quantum groups $C_U($$ ra{g}$)$ and $C_M($$ ra{g}$)$ are identical if the corresponding groups $U($$ra{g}$)$ and $M($$ra{g}$)$ have the same split property. This means all quasi-split inclusions are covered under this equivalence. Additionally, we establish a formula to calculate the quantum group unitary for any given finite-dimensional representation of $M($$ra{g}$)$.

Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for many states. Informed by its relation to the semismooth Newton method and the efficiency of its inexact variations, inexact policy iteration, a class of algorithms for large-scale finite MDPs with local contraction guarantees, was introduced. This method is further exemplified through inexact GMRES policy iteration, which applies GMRES for the policy evaluation process. Notably, inexact GMRES policy iteration outperforms policy iteration and optimistic policy iteration by 5.8 and 2.2 times, respectively, in a 10000-state MDP.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit equal behavior.

This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem presented by expensive computer simulations of complex real-life scenarios. Specifically, researchers focused on an expensive hydrological model designed to generate realistic data for Athens, Georgia, USA. To efficiently handle the large datasets produced by such simulators, an approach involves first selecting key points to approximate the output, and then applying a specialized method to estimate optimal input parameters at those points, while accounting for any uncertainty in the solution. A comprehensive simulation-based study compares the proposed technique with other established methods on a range of synthetic and real-world scenarios.

Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable learnability of complex concepts when evaluating a robust model's accuracy and considering the influence of random example exposure, according to the JvM bound. Specifically, having access to local membership queries or the ability to draw clean examples typically suffices. The implication is that a robust model's learning process may be more resource-intensive compared to a model trained using labeled data. The question then arises as to whether the use of local membership queries is an inherent requirement for achieving robustness. To address this, a new algorithm is proposed, NoLookUp, which eschews the reliance on local membership queries in order to achieve example exposure efficiency, thereby demonstrating the first instance of robust learning achieved through random example exposure alone. NoLookUp works by leveraging a distributionally robust loss function to reduce concept complexity and does not require any distributional assumption regarding the data generating process. The algorithm's robustness is validated through analysis of a modified generalization bound, which demonstrates the influence of random example exposure in achieving robustness. The theoretical findings are substantiated by both empirical and practical observations, which show that NoLookUp can successfully achieve robust learning in real-world scenarios.

For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a lone photon have been measured in both proton-lead collisions and lead-lead collisions. The analysis utilized data from the ATLAS detector for proton-lead collisions with a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV and for lead-lead collisions with a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of 2.76 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets linked with a high-energy photon have been contrasted with those of jets alone, focusing on modifications resulting from the interactions with the medium and from variations in the kinematic factors. The study found that fragmentation functions for jets associated with a high-energy photon exhibit a distinct fragmentation shape compared to jets alone, focusing on modifications above medium effects. Additionally, fragmentation functions for jets with high pT linked to a high-energy photon showed a noticeable increase in low hadron pT and in dense systems, but no notable increase in the dense systems for jets with low pT linked to a high-energy photon.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating central binomial series could be solved using level four multiple zeta values, we now show that alternating versions require level eight and can be solved using an alternative approach. This involves the substitution of hyperbolic trigonometric 1-forms for their standard trigonometric counterparts.

Follow-up research on WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, initially reported by Meisner et al in 2020, has yielded an inventory of its photometric measurements from 1999 to 2019. Although these measurements show variability, the source's spectral type remains uncertain due to conflicting information from different datasets. A study utilizing the source's spectral energy distribution, taking into account data from 2019, places it at 13-16 dorsal magnitudes. Utilizing the source's near-infrared spectrum from 2019, the work presents a model consisting of two co-rotating cool dwarves with temperatures of 650K and 800K respectively. According to the source's light curve, the temperature of one of the dwarves in the system is estimated to be around 780K. The source's variability characteristics match those of binary systems comprised of cool dwarves and/or brown dwarves. The source exhibits color indices similar to those of WISEA J006500.82+425704.85 - the first Y dwarf discovered, identified as a brown dwarf binary system consisting of two objects with temperatures of 300K and 520K. The source's variability pattern is consistent with that of the Y dwarf WISEA J006500.82+425704.85, placed on the brown dwarf Y spectrum sequence. The source's variability pattern is similar to that of binary systems comprised of two objects with large temperature disparities. The source

The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV,
newly calculated using the ATLAS detector at the LHC, is reported for different
centrality ranges and collision outcomes with 10N or fewer charged particles.
These findings demonstrate a significant increase in the number of produced
particles with increasing centrality and, for certain particles, this trend
follows the predicted pattern of rising transverse momentum (pT) distribution
as a function of particle production multiplicity. Particle production
distributions in pT also exhibit distinct differences, with, for example, pions
and kaons displaying branching patterns influenced by both resonance feed-down
and kinematic effects, whereas $\phi$ mesons show no such influence, and
protons show signs of both effects and a contribution from other sources such
as secondary interactions.

We develop a novel, numerically efficient approach to solving DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions by leveraging Chebyshev interpolation techniques. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points for PDF evolution, achieving improved efficiency. The DPD evolution process utilizes a cost-effective grid-point scheme, enabling the incorporation of two distinct renormalization scales for each parton. The proposed methods account for NNLO DGLAP kernels and encompass all relevant flavor combinations.

additive manufacturing technique has the potential to revolutionize the construction of habitats and structures on other planets and moons by turning regolith into building materials.  The key to making regolith-based 3D printing successful lies in finding an appropriate sintering temperature that achieves sufficient strength in the final product.  Using X-ray Computed Tomography and four-point bending tests, researchers studied the mechanical properties and internal structures of samples sintered at various temperatures.  The findings showed that Lunar and Martian regolith reach their optimal sintering range between 575-675 C, resulting in compressive strengths of up to 59 MPa.  The analysis of sample porosity revealed a direct correlation between sintering temperature and reduced void space, ultimately leading to improved material performance.  Applying high-pressure water jet technology to simulate high-stress conditions in off-world environments, researchers subjected samples to 10 MPa pressure, discovering that Lunar and Martian regolith achieve the necessary criteria for structural integrity in the 575-675 C sintering range.  The study's findings provide essential insights for developing scalable and efficient additive manufacturing processes for planetary bases and habitats.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model in a previously unpublished note (in Spanish), but for the sake of completeness and in accordance with journal guidelines, a more comprehensive explanation is presented in this paper. Key aspects include the analysis of steady-state states, stability, and dynamic behaviors resulting from initial perturbations in a problem involving capillary forces and gravity. The obtained solutions reveal how slip at the liquid-solid interface influences the film's behavior, leading to significant variations in critical parameters and instability patterns compared to a scenario with fully wet boundaries. Moreover, the model's predictions have been validated through numerical simulations, which further illustrate the complex behavior of perturbings in a regime influenced by gravity.

By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that measures the recombination of hydrogen in galaxies, our analysis reveals that predictions based on assuming a single type of star emission are accurate enough to meet the needs of current observations. However, this assumption holds only by chance, and and accurate models require consideration of varying star ages. Additionally, our analysis points out discrepancies between observed and predicted data at a specific wavelength, which may potentially impact measurements of galaxy evolution.

This is the initial paper in a series that aims to classify the braided auto-equivalences of the modules in any logarithmic category $ \mathcal{C}$ with at most four exceptions. We begin by establishing a practical method to achieve this goal. The method involves creating a section for the equivariantization of the braided tensor category $ \mathcal{C}$, which we refer to as $ \mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{eq}}$. The section enables us to precisely determine the braided auto-equivalences of $ \mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{eq}}$. We then leverage this determination to identify the braided auto-equivalences of $ \mathcal{C}$. The results obtained in this approach allow us to enumerate the exceptions in a comprehensive list.

The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher for modelling allele spread within genetic populations, but also gained applications by Kolmogorov for a broader range of scenarios. Applying an innovative approach for tackling non-linear partial differential equations provides a distinctive approximate solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, however, defies initial intuition. Although the solution appears to violate fundamental principles, it adheres to established standards for validity in the respective mathematical framework.

This work addresses the UbiComp 2021 Challenge presented by Stabilo, aiming to classify handwritten mathematical terms based on time series data from the DigiPen. The challenge involves recognizing mathematical expressions from 15 possible characters written by multiple individuals. To overcome the initial challenge, a data-driven and rule-based information extraction technique is applied to break down the labeled data. Following this process, two machine learning models are developed - the first is a binary classifier leveraging a hybrid Deep Neural Network and Random Forest to detect writing activities, and the second is a Deep Neural Network integrating convolutional and recurrent layers for single-character classification. Although the proposed approach demonstrates satisfactory accuracy, it fails to fully meet the challenge's requirements due to a notable discrepancy in detection and classification accuracies.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling a form of output regularization. Compared to prior methods, this approach yields improved median speech durations, as well as better quality and more natural-sounding speech, according to subjective evaluations.

Species distribution analysis can be effectively conducted through occupancy modeling, taking into consideration inaccuracies in species detection data. To address multiple species, states, items of observational data, and non-detection data, we have developed a versatile framework. This framework is capable of handling a wide range of detection processes and can be expanded to include covariates that influence species occurrence and detection probabilities. Utilizing a data augmentation approach, we have developed an efficient Markov Chain Monte Carlo estimation method that accommodates uncertain species presence at the site level through a Bayesian switching-state model. This method enables seamless incorporation of non-detection data, enhancing species occurrence inference. The framework's utility can be extended to address various research questions by strategically selecting special cases through plausible priors. The framework's performance will be compared with alternative methods in simulated data and real-world datasets.

Due to the accessibility of smartphones and the increasing reliance on remote healthcare services, diagnosing diseases using image recognition on mobile devices has become increasingly vital. However, the limitations of mobile devices' processing power mean that complex deep learning models cannot be deployed without significant compromises on performance. Our research introduces a novel interactive deep learning framework, known as DARTHOUN, which utilizes human computation to enhance mobile-based medical diagnosis on a macro scale. By engaging users in the diagnosis process, DARTHOUN gathers additional information, allowing it to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy in diagnosing malignant skin lesions, outperforming existing mobile-based approaches by 8.5%. Furthermore, our system's interactive design enhances user experience while minimizing the computational burden on mobile devices.

To capture the intrinsic variability of type Ia supernovae from limited spectral data, we developed a probabilistic autoencoder that incorporates a Normalizing Flow component after initial training using an Auto-Encoder. The model's two-stage generative architecture represents a supernova's physics-based classification and residual variability. The pre-trained Auto-Encoder compresses spectral data into low-dimensional space, mapping diverse supernovae spectra. A subsequent Normalizing Flow module transforms this compressed data into a probability distribution over the supernova parameter space. We applied the model to synthetic data sets, exploring its ability to identify rare events within populations of supernovae. The PAE successfully reconstructed spectral data at or below z=0.3 from the SPEC-II data set with an RMS residual of 0.067 dex in magnitude. Notably, the model achieved an incredible 99.9% accuracy in classifying rare events within a population of supernovae when provided with data from just 10 events. When trained on spectra with diverse signal-to-noise ratios, the model showed no significant dependence on signal-to-no-noise ratio, indicating its robustness under different data conditions. The model was even able to identify population-level differences in supernova evolution times for two distinct peak brightness magnitudes.
