Many software systems have adjustable settings that can be modified at run-time to optimize their performance, reliability, and efficiency. Nonetheless, varying these settings also leads to unintended consequences, such as creating incompatible system configurations or producing low-quality results. To mitigate such issues, we can produce in-depth reports outlining the optimal system settings required to meet specific criteria. We can accomplish this by using learning models trained on data collected from benchmark tests, which measure how different settings impact a system's performance, reliability, and efficiency. We apply our approach to Ruby, a widely used programming language, and use it to produce reports for several prominent libraries, showing that system configurations can be optimized to achieve significant improvements (up to 25% smaller binaries) with minimal code modifications.

Light dark matter particles, particularly those weighing less than a GeV, offer an attractive option over heavier, weakly-interacting massive particles. Directly detecting such lightweight particles, however, poses a significant challenge. But if the recoil of a struck nucleus leads to electron ionization, even if the recoil itself is too subtle to be measured, it's still possible to detect the released electron. This process has been effectively utilized in experiments testing for electric dipole moments. In areas where the recoil threshold is high, detectors may be able to identify the space where the recoil nucleus resides. By combining the likelihood of the electron's position and the ionization characteristics, it's possible to constrain dark matter models more tightly.

This paper proposes a method to produce the most connected pairs of qubit states
via an anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction system, resulting in maximally entangled
anti-polariton qubits. The study reveals that in the initial absence of any photons,
the quantum fluctuations of the anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction behave in the opposite
direction of the standard Jaynes-Cummings interaction process and the rate at which
these states become entangled has a similar pattern in both processes. Furthermore,
utilizing this maximally connected state and entanglement swapping, a near perfect
transfer of an atomic quantum state via quantum teleportation is demonstrated.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBI from raw ECG signals is challenging due to noise and non-linear transformations. Traditional time-frequency analysis methods have limitations in identifying the heart rate variability feature. This study presents a new approach based on the modified Stockwell transform to improve the identification of IBI from noisy ECG signals, and we compare it with existing methods of time-frequency analysis.

We analyze large deviations of power input by an active force on an Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) within or outside a confinement. Analytical calculations of the rate function are done for the free particle in any dimension using a saddle-point expansion. Additionally, numerical evaluations of the rate function are performed for the free particle in two and three dimensions, as well as for the particle in a harmonic potential well in two dimensions. These analyses reveal that the impact of activity coefficient varies significantly depending on the dimension and confinement type. Moreover, the results show that the long-time behavior of the averaged power input closely tracks the behavior of the AOUP.

This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset showcasing diverse human body expressions while accounting for everyday attire. The primary goal of HUMBI is to enhance modeling accuracy by capturing five essential bodily signals, such as gaze, facial expressions, hand gestures, posture, and clothing variations across a range of subjects. The creation of HUMBI involves utilizing 107 high-definition synchronized video cameras to capture and synthesize a total of 5810 minutes of high-definition footage, capturing subtle and intricate aspects of human body language. The proposed system utilizes 108 multi-view skeletal trackers derived from 3D pose estimations to provide a complete understanding of human body expressions from various viewpoints. The integration of advanced data processing and editing techniques allows for the generation of realistic, volume-rich HD human bodies that can be synthesized from the captured skeletal data, expanding the scope of HUMBI to encompass metamodeling capabilities. The resulting dataset presents a substantial advancement over existing human body language datasets, as HUMBI outperforms other datasets in terms of population diversity, demonstrating a 2.5 times greater variety, as well as a significant improvement in model complexity, with a 4.5 times more detailed articulation. The comprehensive metadata included in HUMBI featuring extensive annotations enables seamless integration with leading human body models, such as SMPL and SMPL-X. The public release of HUMBI provides a framework for comprehensive benchmarking, enabling evaluation of a broad range of body language tasks and

Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing has long been dominated by English, due in part to the scarcity of large, high-quality datasets in these languages. Our approach tackles this issue by transferring neural models from English to other languages, utilizing a multilingual pre-trained language model and a custom framework that accommodates cross-lingual transfer. Our general framework is applicable to all tasks and languages, and can be expanded to any task or language with a HuggingFace transformer model. Our results show that this framework is particularly effective for low-resource languages such as Spanish, French, and German, and can also improve performance in high-resource languages like Japanese and Korean when used to augment existing datasets.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature aggregation. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the development of a more sophisticated video super-resolution model. By introducing this enhancement, we create the BVS-RNet model, which surpasses all variants of BasicVSR in metric performance and achieves the best results among state-of-the-art methods with a significantly reduced number of parameters.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-room Vizdoom
scenarios.

We have improved the performance of heat engines working within specific timeframes, employing a time-varying energy function in conjunction with experimentally grounded limitations on the bath temperature and the scale factor. A broadly applicable geometric proof demonstrates that a universally efficient protocol, independent of the system's dynamics, achieves optimal efficiency when subject to these practical constraints. For systems subject to pairwise interactions and multiple scale factors, we have theoretically identified all naturally efficient protocols, which take the form of cyclic trajectories in phase space that are invariant to the scale factor. These universal protocols are applicable to a wide range of physical systems, such as spin chains and magnetic nanoparticles.

This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding storm surge situations are developed based on actual hurricane parameters. To assess potential losses, the study employs a quantitative metric that estimates total load reduction, and these outcomes are calculated using a simulated model of the 2000-bus Texas power system superimposed onto an actual map of the region. Simulation results indicate that power substations experiencing storm surge-related flooding may incur additional losses as the hurricane continues to move inland.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially developed as simplified models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. We identify that the intrinsic encoding properties of these maps align with those of the Dyck system from the study of languages, and this correspondence serves as the foundation for an in-depth analysis of their invariant measures. Through initial investigation, we confirm the existence of two distinct ergodic measures with maximal entropy for these generalized baker maps, and also reveal the underlying cause for the failure of certain entropy-based approaches.

Following the groundbreaking detection of the Higgs boson in 2012, the field of particle physics has entered an exciting period. A pressing concern is whether the Standard Model of particle physics adequately accounts for the scalar sector observed in nature or if it is a subset of a more complex model featuring additional particles. A critical method for resolving this query involves scrutinizing extended scalar models using future high-energy collider facilities, including the potential proton-proton collider with 27 and 100 TeV center-of-mass energy, and advanced lepton colliders at various energy levels.

This paper introduces a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN produces highly realistic, high-quality audio by utilizing a stack of dilated convolution layers with exponential moving average (EMA). However, the lack of pitch in WN restricts its utilization in sequence-to-sequence conditional synthesis. The proposed QPNet builds upon WN and incorporates EMA at multiple levels, including input, hidden, and convolution layers, to capture recurring patterns in input features. The model's pitch dependence is achieved by applying an encoder with a recurrent unit, connected to a vector quantizer and an EMA gateway that feeds information to WN. The experiments demonstrate that QPNet outperforms both a pitch-conditioned WaveNet and a quasi-periodic unit-based WaveNet in terms of inference time, and produces the best quality among these models in terms of Mel cepstral coefficients (MCEs) for a speech synthesis task.

Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the dominant method, have become an integral part of our daily lives as consumers. However, their limitations become apparent when dealing with recommendations for unknown users or items. Traditional solutions struggle with these challenges, but they require extensive knowledge of the system's parameters to function optimally. In contrast, our proposed method - the Burg BF (Burg's Flat Spectra CF) - leverages an approach inspired by signal processing to address the unknowns in CF, relying on autocorrelation and spectral analysis rather than any system-specific parameters. This framework works by transforming the CF problem into a spectral analysis task, applying the Burg algorithm to auto-convolution matrices and deriving feature vectors. The Burg BF features are then used in a metric-free similarity measurement system, demonstrating superior performance in dealing with the unknowns and showcasing a strong potential for general applicability across various domains.

Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these signals from a planet's Doppler signal. In this research, we studied the spectral features of stellar magnetic activity using data from the HARPS-N solar telescope at 450 nm, analyzing the variations in line shifts and line depths. By applying a dimensionality reduction technique, we mapped the multi-dimensional data onto a two-dimensional graph, where distinct periods of activity were detected, spanning several days. By comparing the features of active regions, we found that stars with magnetic activity exhibit different characteristics compared to the neutral infrared line of the sun. Furthermore, these features enable us to differentiate between stellar activity and the planet's signal, demonstrating the potential to identify planet signals hidden by activity.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method measures the ratio of tunneling conductance at non-zero temperatures to its conductance at zero temperature. The method was tested on a hybrid system consisting of a InAs nanowire nanosensor and verified to distinguish between a Majorana peak and those caused by proximity-induced Majorana domains or zero-energy peaks formed by backscattering within a topologically non-trivial nanowire. The results showed that the tunneling conductance exhibits distinct temperature dependencies, with the Majorana peak growing as temperature decreases as a result of temperature-dependent changes in the Fermi energy, whereas the other peaks shift away from zero energy as temperature decreases.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it becomes evident that the Morita invariance holds for strict monoidal categories, and this paper establishes the strict monoidal categories' invariance under the influence of shadows, thereby providing an axiomatic characterization of Morita invariance within this context.

Existing approaches to image editing tasks like color grading often yield multiple possible outcomes rather than a single definitive result, as numerous different styles are applicable to these operations. Current machine learning-based methods typically disregard this stylistic variability in their pursuit of identifying a unique solution. We contend that stylistic diversity is essential to drawing inspiration from human color grading techniques. To address this, we propose a novel generative modeling technique that accounts for multiple possible outcomes in image editing tasks. We apply this framework to the challenge of color grading, developing a generative model that accurately replicates various color grading styles while also maintaining the input-image's overall layout. We experiment with our model in an unsupervised setting, leveraging it to produce a range of color grading styles identified as "film style," "television style," and "social media style."

This technical report reviews the winning approaches to the tasks addressed in the RealWorld Robust Video Understanding Challenge at the CVPR 2021 conference. The RealWorld Robust Video Understanding Challenge focused on developing methods to effectively handle real-world video understanding issues such as occlusion, object movement, vanishing points, and a significant increase in data volume compared to traditional short-form video datasets. To overcome these challenges, participants had to develop techniques to model temporal relationships, improve vanishing point handling, reduce occlusion effects, and achieve data scale scalability. This report will detail the shared strategies and distinctive approaches used by the top competitors to overcome these obstacles and achieve high accuracy on tasks such as multi-step temporal aggregation, semantic joint segmentation, and semantic joint tracking.

This field research focuses on snow deposition dynamics by monitoring the atmospheric flow and snowfall patterns. Using a polarized camera, we capture polarized light reflected off snowflakes in a falling flux, which allows us to analyze their orientation and dimension. This gives us insight into the relationship between snowflakes, the position of the sun, and polarization properties, and we utilize that information to obtain the 3D orientation of falling snowflakes. Additionally, our approach enables the identification of vortex structures in the atmospheric flow, which influences snowflake alignment and settling behavior, and provides a method to calculate snowflake dimensions and orientation without relying on the sunlight's position.

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool for navigating uncertainty, but it poses a challenge to explain how two identical brains cooperate to tackle shared tasks. Our research offers a solution to this challenge by proposing a straightforward method for explaining how similar brains work together to overcome uncertainty. This approach involves each brain sharing information with others through a process of mutual communication. When applied to a basic model, the results show that the information shared allows for successful coordination on challenging tasks, such as reaching for objects, even in the presence of distractions. This theory provides a framework for understanding how interconnected brains tackle complex problems.

In experimental facilities specializing in high energy physics, nuclear physics, and cosmology, the task of analyzing large datasets in real-time poses significant challenges. As a result, there is an increasing interest in developing intelligent data analysis techniques that can facilitate real-time data processing. Consequently, researchers are introducing the concept of Deep Learning (DL) into the analysis pipeline, despite its substantial computational requirements. To address these issues, this paper explores the integration of DL models onto Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), which feature a unique hardware architecture ideal for handling parallel data flows. The authors thoroughly evaluate various FPGA architectures in terms of their suitability for handling different types of neural network architectures. Furthermore, a practical implementation of an Inertial Neutrino Observer, designed to analyze neutrino data, is demonstrated using two different FPGAs.

Utilizing Finzi's gravity theory that enhances interactions at large scales, we analyze galaxy clusters from a thermodynamic perspective, establishing a statistical model to derive thermodynamic equations and comparing clustering behavior with Newtonian gravity. This approach enables us to scrutinize the influence of the theory's parameter on the cluster scale.

A type of convex geometric hypergraph, known as cgh, comprises a set of subsets originating from strictly convex point sets in the plane. In this study, researchers explore a specific type of problem associated with cghs: saturation problems that correspond to earlier studied extremal issues. Using a mathematical approach, the study determines the maximum capacity of certain geometrically separated groups of points and establishes an exact value for a specific instance, as well as approximate values for seven out of eight possible geometric hypergraph configurations up to a specific level of accuracy, and a lower bound for the eighth configuration.

To gain a better understanding of the relative importance of different reaction channels, a detailed analysis was conducted on the ground state and isobaric analytic state components of $\alpha$-particle angular distributions resulting from $d$-wave resonances in a number of $^{6}$Li+$^{51}$V, $^{7}$Li+$^{51}$V, and $^{7}$Li+$^{51}$Cr collisions between 72.5 MeV and 90 MeV lab energy. Calculations employing a coupled channels optical model and coupled reaction calculus framework revealed that the contributions of non-resonant $s$ and $p$-wave channels to alpha production far exceed that of the $d$-wave channels, which were studied in this research. It was also observed that the optical model can effectively account for a substantial portion of the non-resonant data, with the findings indicating that the primary channels responsible for alpha production are the non-resonant $s$ and $p$-channel elastic and inelastic processes. Specifically, the 1st and 2nd $s$-wave and 1st $p$-wave non-resonant elastic and inelastic channels collectively explain the majority of the experimental angular distribution shapes and magnitudes measured in this research, with the corresponding optical model parameters displaying significant correlation for the channels studied, particularly for the $s$-wave channels. With the parameter ranges observed, the contribution of the non-resonant processes

A previously overlooked ability in bio-inspired snake robots is dynamic vertical climbing. A novel locomotion technique mimicking the Pacific Lamprey's movement has been discovered, which enables a robot to navigate on flat surfaces while climbing at near-vertical inclines. A simplified model of this movement has been created and successfully implemented in a robot called Trident. The robot features a unique head section that can move independently, allowing it to navigate on flat surfaces and climb at angles of up to 86 degrees. The head section travels along a track that is parallel to the surface, and the robot's body undulates to achieve the necessary movement. Tests have demonstrated that Trident can achieve dynamic vertical climbs at speeds of 4.3 cm/s and transition between flat surface movement and climbing in less than 2 seconds.

This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the colon cancer dynamics, whose probabilistic evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. To identify optimal treatment combinations, an open-loop control optimization issue is proposed. Simulation results demonstrating the use of Doxorubicin chemotherapy and IL-2 immunotherapy validate the introduced framework.

Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication success depends heavily on minimizing excessive interference and ensuring high data transmission rates. Achieving this goal requires a precise balance between scheduling D2D pairs and managing their interactions. To tackle this challenge, we propose an innovative approach, which involves using a two-stage process in a next-generation 5G wireless network. Firstly, we employ a nonlinear, multi-objective optimization technique to maximize the overall network throughput, minimize interference, and extend battery life. To handle this complex optimization, we utilize an evolutionary algorithm and an efficient data structure. Subsequently, we utilize a graph theory tool to assign a specific scheduling strategy to each D2D pair, which involves packaging multiple communication tasks onto a single path, which results in significant reductions in interference and improves overall network performance. To validate our approach, we conduct extensive simulations within a variety of outdoor environments. The results show that our technique outperforms existing methods in terms of throughput, interference, and energy efficiency.

Moffatt first discussed the concept of helicity in a fluid without viscosity in reference [25] and explored its preservation in the case of barotropic, compressible flow with smooth solutions. This paper demonstrates that weak solutions to this system in a specific mathematical space ensure the conservation of helicity. Additionally, similar results were found for both homogeneous incompressible Euler equations and the surface quasi-geostrophic equation.

The researchers in a particular study extended the solutions found in complex geometric optics to a related system of equations, which was initially investigated in contexts of electrical impedance tomography and the integrable Davey-Stewartson II equations, focusing particularly on the large spectral parameter $k$ in a specified reference \cite{KlSjSt20}. They now examined how this work can be applied to the reflection coefficient and derived new asymptotic formulas for specific domains with potential functions and smooth, strictly convex boundaries.

Calculations involving the orbital dynamics of merging compact binary systems,
accouting for gravitational wave effects in the binary's final orbits, have been
conducting for the first time. These studies considered two objects of equal mass
inspiraling down due to gravitational interactions, with no spin. The analysis used
models from the 2+1 general relativity framework, which incorporate the effects of
gravitational radiation-reaction throughout the binary's inspiral and merger.
Results show significant variations in the final binary's orbital characteristics
at lower frequency ranges compared to predictions from standard general relativity models.
The findings suggest that accounting for gravitational radiation effects could lead
to greater production of gravitational waves in binary systems like PSR B1913+16.

A proposed innovation combines the benefits of X-ray free-electron laser oscillators (XFELOs) and the undulator taper technique to create a groundbreaking X-ray laser. This XFELO with tapering (XFT) design is expected to achieve unprecedented pulse durations and high average power, thereby increasing the gain bandwidth and making it more stable to perturbations. The outcome will be a more robust and reliable XFT laser, enabling precise control over its parameters and potentially leading to a major advance in experimental applications.

Event identification is crucial for informed decision-making in graph data analysis systems.  Graph-based machine learning has made significant advancements lately, but detecting events in evolving networks still poses difficulties for current frameworks. Real-world occurrences typically involve sudden changes in network behavior patterns. Traditional methods for dynamic graph analysis, such as focusing on key nodes or overall network patterns, can be ineffective in capturing event-related information. This paper introduces an approach to address this limitation by incorporating sudden changes in network behavior into an event detection algorithm. We develop a method that identifies abrupt shifts in network features and leverages clustering techniques to group connected nodes together. We apply this approach to a real-world problem of security threat detection within an air transportation system.

The solutions of the Guderley problem involving an imploding shock wave in an ideal gas are examined, focusing on how a power law initial density distribution affects the accelerating shock. This is achieved through in-depth analysis of self-similar solutions and their similarity exponents under different symmetry conditions and varying parameters of adiabatic index and spatial density exponent. Moreover, we show how these theoretical solutions can be accurately reproduced in Lagrangian hydrodynamic simulations, thereby validating and verifying these codes for a range of scenarios.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field will be highlighted and solutions proposed, with a framework and future research directions on how requirements engineering can aid in addressing these difficulties.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 953k images (23.5Gb), comprising various stains and histological masks for colorectal polyps, gathered from 2,031 glass slides. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers to develop and test algorithms for automating colorectal histopathology, with additional information on gynecological tumors and tests. UniToPatho is now available for public use at https://datashare.isc.cnr.it/UnitoPatho/.

In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. When the adversary follows a random guessing strategy, this quantity translates to the maximum amount of entropy lost in the source coding process. Previous studies had established upper limits for this quantity, and we introduce new distributional criteria that guarantee these upper limits can be achieved. Specifically, our work shows that these limits can be realized by conforming to two strict standards: the encoded sequence must be both uniquely identifiable and exponentially rare.

Deep learning-based generative models, specifically VAEs and GANs, can learn a compressed, low-dimensional representation of data, allowing for the recovery of images from limited measurements, like sparse or noisy data. Our code, called pyGENSOM, provides an easy-to-use platform for VAEs and GANs, offering a user-friendly interface to learn and utilize these models for image reconstruction tasks. The platform includes a variety of features to streamline the process, including a customizable interface for selecting and configuring generative models, a user-friendly data structure for managing and preprocessing data, and a range of functions for reconstructing images from limited data. The code is extensively documented with tutorials and examples that demonstrate how to use the platform effectively.

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical strategy to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  To optimize this approach, a critical factor is the optimal settings for its quantum parameters.  The conventional markov chain Monte Carlo method has shown efficiency in this context, but it entails significant computational costs.  A new approach presented here leverages a more cost-effective unsupervised data-driven strategy using normalized predictive control.  This strategy relies on real-time running data to adjust the QAOA parameters without requiring extensive modeling.  The proposed method's performance is compared to the markov chain Monte Carlo method in several optimization challenges.  Resulting findings indicate the proposed method's capability to locate efficient operating points for the QAOA algorithm, yielding superior results in comparison to the markov chain Monte Carlo method.  Moreover, this strategy is adaptable across various scenarios, including those with constrained variables.

A versatile method has been devised for determining the overlap area between two ellipses. The proposed approach relies on computing segment areas between the two ellipses, using a secant line that intersects each ellipse at given points. The Gauss-Green formula enables calculation of an ellipse sector area, with a triangle either added to or subtracted from this sector area to obtain the segment area. For calculating the overlap area of two ellipses, the areas of relevant sectors and polygons are combined. The algorithm identifies the intersection points of two ellipses by solving two quartic equations, resulting in a complex expression that can be simplified using algebraic properties to obtain a and b in terms of the ellipse parameters. The identified intersection points are then used to compute the overlap area using the above-mentioned segment area formula. The proposed method enables the efficient computation of overlap areas between two general ellipses in a Cartesian coordinate system.

Building upon the work by Wang et al. (2020) for reinforcement learning, we examine the continuous-time counterpart of Q-learning under the assumption of a spatially homogeneous Markov model. The theory develops mathematical connections between the q-function, a function that maps states to actions, and an "instantaneous advantage rate function". It demonstrates that the q-function can be expressed as the stochastic integral of the instantaneous advantage rate function with respect to the conditional mean field. Furthermore, we present stochastic gradient algorithms for estimating the q-function and "instantaneous advantage rate function". The theoretical findings are substantiated by numerical simulations that demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms.

Quantum magnets on triangular and kagome lattices possess inherent magnetic frustration, making them suitable candidates for spin liquids or hidden-order states. The Hubbard model is crucial in studying these systems, especially when incorporating the effects of doping and spin-orbit coupling. The result is a complex phase diagram featuring various antiferromagnetic patterns and unique excitations.

Using the determinant method, researchers calculate magnetic excitations for the Hubbard model on a triangular lattice with spin-orbit coupling. They find that at half filling, the spectrum exhibits a unique 'flat band' characteristic of a quantum spin Hall state. However, this band vanishes when the system becomes metallic at small doping levels. To understand the origin of these zero modes, the researchers use a mean-field approach and find that they are an inherent consequence of the symmetry of the triangular lattice under continuous spin rotations.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages high-dimensional image features combined with a probabilistic model to support medical doctors in identifying vertebral pathology. Specifically, the proposed approach utilizes a novel key point localization network that integrates multiple scale information to accurately pinpoint vertebral key points, followed by a probabilistic model that incorporates a Markov Random Field model to link these key points and generate the final vertebrae identification results. To evaluate the efficacy of the proposed approach, we established the MIP-Gleno dataset, comprising 50 CT scans with severe spine pathology, and compared it to eight other popular methods. The results revealed that our approach achieved the highest accuracy, outperforming other methods by up to 10.6% in terms of identification precision.

Stochastic thermodynamics leverages Markovian jump processes to simulate chemical reactions, yet traditional methods based on transition probabilities fail to capture the impact of microscopic fluctuations on reaction rates. In contrast, an alternative approach uses ergodic Markov processes driven by Brownian motion to model the macromolecular movements between reactive states. This study applies a new approach to analyze the fluctuations in reaction rates by formulating a scaled cumulant-generating function for stochastic thermodynamics. The results demonstrate that gauge invariance is maintained, which enables the calculation of variance and skewness in reaction rates without compromising the approach's versatility. This gauge-invariant method can be applied to systems influenced by external forces and/or temperature gradients, which may vary both spatially and temporally.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means, yielding an explicit match up to a multiplicative factor.

Two piezoelectric materials placed near each other can transfer energy across an intervening vacuum gap by transmitting acoustic waves. Our research provides a mathematical explanation for how this energy transfer occurs, and reveals that specific conditions allow for complete transmission of these waves. This finding holds true for materials of any shape or orientation and can be determined experimentally through measurement of surface properties. Furthermore, we analyzed the optimal energy transfer between identical zinc oxide crystals for various orientations and found a significant number of conditions that facilitate energy transmission.

We explore a cutting-edge method for optically manipulating polariton condensates at a microscale, relying on highly coherent light sources produced by semiconductor lasers or advanced light-matter interaction techniques. By strategically positioning a thin-layered nonlinear crystal near the polariton condensate, it's possible to redirect the condensate's emission in a controlled manner. However, this redirection process requires a sophisticated understanding of spatial light manipulation techniques. In our study, we've successfully demonstrated the ability to focus the polariton condensate's emission into a tiny point, achieving a high transmission rate of 85% for a specific wavelength. This breakthrough has the potential to significantly improve optical communication systems, enable faster data transfer, and open up new avenues for research on faster-than-light data transfer concepts.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b displays erratic patterns in its transit light curve. Different theories attempt to explain its origin, including disintegration, erosion, and accretion processes. To gain insight, we examine the environmental factors that could be contributing to its disintegration. We find that an upper limit exists for the planet's internal temperature, potentially reached by any internal energy source, and control of thermal flux, thereby dictating the temperature of the upper mantle. Depending on the presence of a supercritical water cycle, this upper limit could be as low as 300 K. We also model the atmospheric escape of the planet, limited by a new estimate of the kinetic energy per unit mass of the flow, and find that even minimal magnetic induction by the planet can prevent escape above a certain threshold. Based on these findings, we conclude that the environment surrounding the planet K2-22b is likely characterized by a balance between atmospheric escape and accretion, with possible implications for the extant habitability of exoplanets like K2-22b.

We develop a novel algebro-geometric approach to studying the Milnor fibration and establish a significant condition for holomorphic function deformations to maintain the Milnor fibration intact. In consequence, we derive a strategy to divide the space of polynomials with a specified degree into discrete, localized segments where the diffeomorphism of the Milnor fibration remains unchanged within each category.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform library focused on data analysis and scientific computing with data frames at its core. Designed for.NET environments, this library seamlessly integrates with popular tools like U2DC and MATLAB, while maintaining complete compatibility with the.NET Data Analytics Framework. Daany boasts an array of features, including data manipulation, statistical analysis, matrix operations, least squares calculations, PCA, regression analysis, and optimization algorithms, all built upon the matrix-based concept. Developed under the MIT license, this library is entirely free, making it an ideal solution for data-driven applications requiring efficient data analysis.

I challenge the conventional view of Galileo's influence on science by suggesting that he struggled with mathematical proficiency. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic scientific principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics, as they often say "those who can't do, teach." It is proposed that Galileo's scientific vision, which is typically viewed as groundbreaking, was, in fact, based on long-established ideas from mathematicians such as Bonaventura Cavalieri. His failure to fully integrate his scientific and mathematical skills might have ultimately led to his inability to develop a unified, mathematical physics, as seen in the work of Isaac Newton.

The increasing popularity of Tsallis' thermodynamic framework stems from its capability to describe phenomena exhibiting anomalous thermal properties, which requires adherence to generalized energy conservation principles. Our investigation extends this approach to 1+1 and 3+1 dimensional quantum field theories in both constant and time-dependent external fields. We derived non-equilibrium grand canonical partition functions for these theories, which we subsequently utilized to calculate classical and quantum ionization processes, such as those encountered in astrophysical contexts. Our findings demonstrate the ionization process can be represented within the context of Tsallis statistics, with the normalization constant exhibiting a connection to the non-extensive temperature parameter. We show that Tsallis statistics is consistent with the AdS/CFT correspondence in constant external fields and discuss implications for quantum plasma research.

The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to investigate the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations only in relevant areas, this novel model enables more efficient computation. The comparative study involves three scenarios: the MHD-AEPIC model, MHD simulations paired with fixed embedded PIC regions, and full PIC simulations. The examination of reconnection rates, magnetic island spacings, and ion dynamics within these scenarios indicates good agreement among the models, with notably large adaptable PIC regions required within the MHD domain to achieve such convergence.

This document provides a summary of the content from a course held at Stanford University in the spring of 2018.  The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence.  The course uses a tangible example - digital assistants that learn and improve with expert input - to explore how these intelligent systems function.  The course consists of 12 lectures that delve into the underlying theories and present them through a unified view of intelligent systems that blend human and machine capabilities.
